# SecMan web-security check

`secman-web-check` is the merged command-line scanner for two selectable approaches:
bounded HTTP/TLS security checks and headless-browser visual exposure checks. Run
either approach independently or run both against the same explicit target set.

Redirect chains are reported hop by hop. Cross-host transitions and blocked downgrade,
invalid, or over-limit redirects receive distinct findings.

> Scan only systems you own or are explicitly authorized to assess. Passive scanning is
> the default. Active requests and access to RFC1918/ULA targets require separate,
> explicit opt-ins.

## Five-minute quickstart

Prerequisites: macOS or Linux, Python 3.12 or newer, and
[`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).

```bash
git clone <repository-url> secman_web_check
cd secman_web_check
./scripts/setup.sh
uv run --locked secman-web-check --help
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com \
  --format all \
  --output-dir scan-output \
  --fail-on none
```

Replace `https://example.com` with an authorized target. The final command performs a
passive HTTP/TLS scan and writes terminal, JSON, SARIF, and self-contained HTML output.
Machine reports are placed below `scan-output/` and contain findings only—never raw
response bodies.

You can also activate the virtual environment and use the installed command directly:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
secman-web-check scan https://example.com
```

## Common examples

Select the scan approach explicitly:

```bash
# HTTP/TLS checks only (the backward-compatible default)
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com --scan-mode security

# Browser screenshot plus vision analysis
SECMAN_VISION_API_KEY='REDACTED' \
  uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com --scan-mode visual

# Security and visual scans in one local report
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com \
  --scan-mode both --visual-no-ai --format all --fail-on none
```

`--visual-no-ai` performs deterministic screenshot capture without a model call, so it
cannot report visual-content findings. Screenshots are written below
`OUTPUT_DIR/screenshots` unless `--visual-output-dir` is supplied. Full-page captures
are capped at 4000 pixels.

Scan one public target using safe defaults:

```bash
./scripts/scan-single.sh https://example.com -- --format terminal
```

Verify redirect reporting with the public HTTP testing endpoint:

```bash
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://httpbin.org/redirect/1 \
  --format json \
  --fail-on none
```

The JSON findings include `WEB-TRANSPORT-REDIRECT` for the observed hop. Redirects to a
different hostname, HTTPS downgrades, and blocked redirects receive additional rule IDs.

Scan the example target list and write every format:

```bash
./scripts/scan-list.sh examples/targets.txt -- \
  --config examples/config.toml \
  --format all \
  --output-dir scan-output \
  --fail-on medium
```

Run the documented active probe allowlist:

```bash
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com --active
```

The `--active` flag enables fixed `TRACE`, `OPTIONS`, `.env`, `.git/HEAD`,
`server-status`, and configuration-backup requests. It does not enable crawling,
arbitrary paths, authentication, exploitation, brute force, or fuzzing.

Scan an authorized private target:

```bash
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://10.20.30.40 \
  --allow-private-targets
```

This flag permits only RFC1918 IPv4 and IPv6 ULA addresses. Loopback, link-local,
multicast, unspecified, documentation, and other special-purpose ranges remain denied.
It does not imply `--active`.

## Targets

Supply exactly one positional target, one `--targets-file`, or one `--targets-csv`.
Hostnames without a scheme use HTTPS. Plain target files are UTF-8, one URL or hostname
per line; blank lines and lines beginning with `#` are ignored, and normalized
duplicates are removed.

```bash
secman-web-check scan example.com
secman-web-check scan https://example.com/application/health
secman-web-check scan --targets-file examples/targets.txt
secman-web-check scan --targets-csv testdata/targets-aws.csv
```

AWS target CSV files use this exact header and one account/target pair per row:

```csv
awsAccountNumber,target
111122223333,https://example.com/
444455556666,service.example.org
```

Account numbers must contain exactly 12 digits. The account number is retained in JSON
reports and narrows SecMan subject matching before URI or hostname matching. A normalized
target cannot be assigned to two different accounts in the same file.

User information, URL fragments, non-HTTP schemes, and denied network addresses are
rejected. Every DNS answer and redirect is revalidated. Approved connections pin the
resolved IP while retaining the hostname for HTTP `Host`, TLS SNI, and certificate
verification.

## Reports and exit codes

`--format` is repeatable and accepts `terminal`, `json`, `sarif`, `html`, or `all`.
Terminal is the default. JSON uses schema version `1.0`; SARIF uses version `2.1.0`;
HTML is self-contained, script-free, escaped, and protected by a restrictive CSP.

`--fail-on` accepts `info`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `critical`, or `none` and defaults
to `high`.

- `0`: scan completed and no finding met the configured threshold.
- `1`: at least one finding met the configured threshold.
- `2`: invalid configuration, a failed/partial target, or an operational adapter error.

See [Report formats](docs/REPORTS.md) for schemas and examples.

## Configuration

Configuration precedence is CLI, `SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_*` environment variables, the
`[scan]` table in a TOML file, then safe defaults. The example config keeps active and
private scanning disabled.

```bash
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan --targets-file examples/targets.txt \
  --config examples/config.toml
```

Secrets are never accepted as CLI values or TOML settings. Vision credentials use
`SECMAN_VISION_API_KEY`; optional `SECMAN_VISION_MODEL` and
`SECMAN_VISION_BASE_URL` select the model/provider. See
[Configuration reference](docs/CONFIGURATION.md).

## Optional MariaDB history

MariaDB access occurs only for `db`, `history`, or a scan with `--store-db`.

```bash
export SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_DB_HOST=db.example.invalid
export SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_DB_USER=scanner_user
export SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_DB_PASSWORD='REDACTED'
export SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_DB_NAME=secman_web_check

uv run --locked secman-web-check db install
uv run --locked secman-web-check db status
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com --store-db
uv run --locked secman-web-check history list --limit 20
```

See [MariaDB setup](docs/DATABASE.md) before applying the example grants.

## Optional SecMan upload

Register separate SecMan scanners for independent lifecycle snapshots: source
`WEB_SECURITY` for security results and source `VISUAL` for visual results. Assign the
same authorized subjects where appropriate. A combined run requires both IDs so one
mode can never resolve findings owned by the other.

```bash
export SECMAN_URL=https://secman.example.invalid
export SECMAN_SECURITY_SCANNER_ID=41
export SECMAN_VISUAL_SCANNER_ID=42
export SECMAN_TOKEN='REDACTED'

uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com --scan-mode both \
  --format json \
  --push-to-secman
```

Uploads use `/api/integrations/v1`, never fall back to legacy ingestion, and submit each
target as an atomic snapshot. Partial or failed coverage never resolves older findings.
See [SecMan integration](docs/SECMAN.md).

To resolve the SecMan credentials with Proton Pass, copy the reference-only example,
replace its item paths, log in once, and use the wrapper. It always enables direct
SecMan upload:

```bash
cp examples/secman-proton-pass.env .env
${EDITOR:-vi} .env
pass-cli login
./scripts/scan-with-proton-pass.sh \
  --targets-csv testdata/targets-aws.csv \
  --format json \
  --output-dir scan-output \
  --fail-on none
```

Use `--env-file FILE` (or `SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_PASS_ENV_FILE`) for another reference file.
`SECMAN_PASS_CLI` may name a non-default `pass-cli` executable. Resolved secrets remain
in the child process environment and are never added to the scanner command line.
The ready-to-edit CSV used above is stored at `testdata/targets-aws.csv`.

For production on AWS, store the same variables as a JSON object in Secrets Manager
and use the normal AWS credential chain (instance role, task role, or workload
identity). The wrapper allowlists environment keys and never prints the returned
secret:

```bash
./scripts/scan-with-aws-secrets.py \
  --secret-id prod/secman/web-check -- \
  https://example.com --scan-mode both --format json --fail-on none
```

## Development and verification

The repository intentionally keeps Python source files directly under `src/`; the build
maps that directory to the installed `secman_web_check` package.

```bash
./scripts/verify.sh
```

The verification script checks the lockfile, tests, Ruff lint/formatting, strict mypy,
the source distribution, and the wheel. Unit tests use deterministic transports and
mock adapters; they do not require a live target, MariaDB instance, or SecMan deployment.

## Documentation

- [Checks and severities](docs/CHECKS.md)
- [Configuration reference](docs/CONFIGURATION.md)
- [Safety and authorization](docs/SAFETY.md)
- [Report formats](docs/REPORTS.md)
- [MariaDB setup](docs/DATABASE.md)
- [SecMan integration](docs/SECMAN.md)

## Limitations

- No crawling, discovery, authentication testing, exploitation, brute force, or
  arbitrary fuzzing. Visual mode executes the selected page in isolated headless
  Chromium with outbound destination checks on every request.
- Active findings use strong bounded signatures but may still require human validation.
- HTTPS targets use SSLyze for the documented TLS capabilities; unavailable individual
  capabilities make the target partial instead of silently clean.
- MariaDB and SecMan behavior is covered with isolated tests here; operators must verify
  connectivity, permissions, TLS trust, and retention policy in their own environment.
# SecMan REST integration

SecMan upload is disabled unless `--push-to-secman` is supplied. This is the direct
result-import path; no separate export/import step is required.

1. Register a `WEB_SECURITY` scanner for security results and a `VISUAL` scanner for
   visual results.
2. Assign their service users and bind only authorized asset subjects.
3. Set `SECMAN_URL` to the HTTPS origin plus `SECMAN_SECURITY_SCANNER_ID` and/or
   `SECMAN_VISUAL_SCANNER_ID` for the selected modes.
4. Set `SECMAN_TOKEN`, or set `SECMAN_USERNAME` and `SECMAN_PASSWORD`.
5. Run a local JSON report first, then repeat with `--push-to-secman`.

The client discovers subjects through
`GET /api/integrations/v1/scanners/{id}/subjects` and submits atomic target snapshots to
`POST /api/integrations/v1/runs`. Matching prefers the normalized URI and falls back to
the canonical hostname. For `--targets-csv`, the 12-digit AWS account number first
narrows the authorized subject list by `cloudAccountId`, preventing a same-hostname
asset in another account from being selected. Missing or ambiguous matches fail safely.
No inventory is created and no legacy endpoint is attempted.

A complete successful target may resolve older absent findings for that scanner/subject.
Partial and failed results set `completeCoverage=false`, so they never resolve older
findings. Stable external IDs and deterministic run keys make a retry idempotent.

TLS verification is mandatory. Authentication failures and response errors are
sanitized; tokens, passwords, cookies, and raw web response bodies are not uploaded.

Security and visual results intentionally use separate scanner registrations. A
combined run submits two atomic snapshots; the merged local report is not uploaded as
a third snapshot. This prevents a security-only run from resolving visual findings, or
the reverse. `SECMAN_SCANNER_ID` remains a compatibility fallback only for a
single-mode run.

## Proton Pass credentials

The wrapper follows SecMan's `scripts/import.sh` pattern: `pass-cli` resolves references
into a child process environment, then the scanner runs with `--push-to-secman`.

```bash
cp examples/secman-proton-pass.env .env
${EDITOR:-vi} .env
pass-cli login
./scripts/scan-with-proton-pass.sh \
  --targets-csv testdata/targets-aws.csv \
  --format json \
  --output-dir scan-output \
  --fail-on none
```

The reference file must resolve `SECMAN_URL`, the scanner ID(s) required by the chosen
mode, and either
`SECMAN_TOKEN` or the pair `SECMAN_USERNAME` and `SECMAN_PASSWORD`. Do not put resolved
passwords or tokens in the file. Select another file with `--env-file FILE` or
`SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_PASS_ENV_FILE`; select another executable with `SECMAN_PASS_CLI`.

## AWS Secrets Manager credentials

For production, store the required variables in one JSON `SecretString`. Supported
keys are the SecMan URL, scanner IDs, token or username/password, and optional vision
provider settings. Then run:

```bash
./scripts/scan-with-aws-secrets.py --secret-id prod/secman/web-check -- \
  https://example.com --scan-mode both --format json --fail-on none
```

The script relies on the standard AWS CLI credential chain, rejects unknown JSON keys,
does not echo the secret response, and passes resolved values only in the child process
environment.

## AWS target CSV

`--targets-csv` accepts UTF-8 CSV with this exact header:

```csv
awsAccountNumber,target
111122223333,https://example.com/
444455556666,service.example.org
```

Each account number must be exactly 12 digits and each target must pass the normal URL
and network-policy validation. Blank targets, unexpected columns, malformed rows, and
the same normalized target assigned to different accounts are rejected before scanning.
The account is included in the JSON report and in the SecMan subject-selection step.
A ready-to-edit example is available at `testdata/targets-aws.csv`.
# MariaDB history

Persistence is disabled unless the operator invokes a database/history command or uses
`--store-db`. MariaDB is the only supported database backend.

1. Review [the example grants](../db/grants.example.sql) and replace every placeholder.
2. Create the database/user with an administrative account outside this tool.
3. Export the scanner's least-privilege connection variables described in
   [CONFIGURATION.md](CONFIGURATION.md).
4. Run `./scripts/install-db.sh`, then `secman-web-check db status`.
5. Add `--store-db` only to scans whose history should be retained.

The schema stores version/checksum metadata, scan runs, explicit targets, normalized
findings, completeness, and sanitized errors. All target-controlled values use DB-API
parameters. A run write is transactional; a failure rolls it back and returns exit code
2 without removing reports already generated on disk.

Use a trusted CA with `SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_DB_SSL_CA` when the database requires TLS. The
scanner never prints or persists the database password.

docs/MCP.md:346:- **`import_user_mappings`** — `mappings` holds up to 1000 entries, each with `email`* plus at least one of `awsAccountId` (12 digits) or `domain`. Optionally starts a risk assessment for the owner of every brand-new AWS account the import introduces: `startRiskAssessment` (bool), `riskAssessmentUseCase` (required when it is true), `riskAssessmentDeadlineDays` (1..3650, default `7`). Returns counts `created`, `createdPending` (user does not exist yet), `skipped`, `errors[]`, plus `newAccounts[]` (`awsAccountId`, `emails`) and `riskAssessments[]` (`awsAccountId`, `ownerEmail`, `riskAssessmentId`, `assessor`, `endDate`, `useCase`, `releaseVersion`, `requirementCount`, `skipped`, `skipReason`, `error`). A `riskAssessments[]` entry carries **either** `error` (the assessment failed) **or** `skipped`/`skipReason` (the pair already had an open assessment — an idempotent no-op; do not report it as a failure). Runs the same code path as REST `POST /api/user-mappings/bulk` and CLI `manage-user-mappings import`, so brand-new-account detection is identical. Assessments are pinned to the ACTIVE requirements release; the call is rejected with `VALIDATION_ERROR` when none exists or it carries no requirements for the use case. `onboardingMode` (`WELCOME_ONLY` | `DIRECT` | `GUIDED`) selects what happens for the owner instead; omitting it falls back to `startRiskAssessment`, which on its own means `DIRECT` with no welcome mail — byte-identical to the behaviour before onboarding modes existed. `sendWelcomeEmail` overrides that, and `questionnaireExpiryDays` (1..90, default 14) sets how long a `GUIDED` link lives. The result gains `onboarding[]` with the same three shapes as `riskAssessments[]`. Combining `startRiskAssessment` with a non-`DIRECT` mode is a `VALIDATION_ERROR`. See `docs/AWS_ACCOUNT_RISK_ASSESSMENT.md` and `docs/ACCOUNT_ONBOARDING.md`.

docs/CHANGELOG.md:7:- **AWS account display names link accounts to workgroups (2026-08-25)** — an account whose `display_name` is `DevOps-x` now belongs to workgroup **`aws-DevOps-x`**: matched exactly (case-insensitively) on the `aws-` prefix, **created** when missing. One implementation, `WorkgroupAccountLinkService`, reached from the import (CLI/REST/MCP `displayName`, after the mappings commit) and from a correction path that re-links from stored names with no file — CLI `manage-user-mappings link-workgroups`, `POST /api/user-mappings/link-workgroup-accounts`, MCP `link_workgroup_aws_accounts`. The name is persisted as `user_mapping.aws_account_name` (V260) and deliberately kept **out** of the unique key. A display name that cannot be a workgroup name is an error row, never a forced creation; already-linked accounts are idempotent no-ops. Also fixed: six workgroup MCP tools were in `LISTING` but not `.CALLING` (listed yet uncallable). `docs/AWS_ACCOUNT_WORKGROUP_LINKING.md`.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:19:- **Web findings identify as findings and group under Webserver (2026-09-17)** — the current-vulnerabilities table now labels its identifier column **CVE/Finding**, reflecting that integration projections use stable finding identities rather than CVE identifiers. New `WEB_SECURITY` findings project `Webserver` into the Product field instead of exposing their internal external IDs there; V266 backfills both active vulnerability projections and the durable `integration_finding.projection_product` used when resolved findings reopen. The change is deliberately source-scoped: `VISUAL`, `GITHUB_AI`, CrowdStrike and manual vulnerabilities retain their existing product values, while the stable `INT:...` projection key remains unchanged for per-finding identity and exceptions. Product filters, statistics, exports, notifications and product-scoped exceptions consequently group these findings under `Webserver`.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:23:- **AWS account display names link accounts to workgroups (2026-08-25)** — an AWS account mapping file already names the team that owns each account (`display_name` in the Cloud Custodian export, a `display_name` column in the CSV exports), and that name was being thrown away at the CLI boundary: `UserMappingCliService.parseFromJson` flattened each account to `{email, awsAccountId}` and the backend's `CSVUserMappingParser` treated the column as an ignorable extra. The rule now implemented in one place — `WorkgroupAccountLinkService` — is that an account whose display name is `DevOps-x` belongs to the workgroup **`aws-DevOps-x`**: matched **exactly** on `"aws-" + display_name`, case-insensitively via `WorkgroupRepository.findByNameIgnoreCase`, and **created** (root level, `createdBy` = the acting ADMIN) when it does not exist. Suffixed variants such as `aws-DevOps-x-rolegreen` are deliberately not matched — a fuzzy rule here would hand an unrelated workgroup's members access to an account's assets, since a link is unified-asset-access **rule #9** (`WorkgroupAwsAccount`), not bookkeeping. Reuse rather than reimplementation: creation goes through `WorkgroupService.createWorkgroup` and assignment through `WorkgroupAwsAccountService.add`, whose `actorId` became nullable (`createdBy` is already nullable since V206's ON DELETE SET NULL) so the automated path can record "no interactive actor" instead of inventing one. Two entry points, both ADMIN-only. **During an import**: `BulkUserMappingEntry` gained `displayName`, carried by CLI `manage-user-mappings import` (JSON and the optional CSV `display_name` column), REST `POST /api/user-mappings/bulk`, MCP `import_user_mappings` and REST `POST /api/import/upload-user-mappings-csv`; linking runs in `UserMappingBulkImportService.execute` **after** the mappings commit, the same ordering rule the notification and onboarding side effects already follow, and is wrapped so a linking failure is reported rather than costing an import that already persisted. **On demand**: the new correction path re-links from what is already stored, with no file involved — CLI `manage-user-mappings link-workgroups [--dry-run]`, REST `POST /api/user-mappings/link-workgroup-accounts`, MCP `link_workgroup_aws_accounts`. That is what makes the display name worth persisting: new `user_mapping.aws_account_name` (**V260**, nullable, not backfilled, indexed) is deliberately **not** part of `uk_user_mapping_composite`, because the name describes the account rather than the identity of the mapping — so a rename updates the row instead of forking a second one, and both import paths refresh the name on rows they skip as duplicates (without that, the correction path would be blind to every account whose mappings already existed). Edge cases are result rows, never exceptions, so one bad account cannot abort a 10,000-account import: a display name that cannot legally be a workgroup name (`Workgroup.name` allows letters, digits, spaces and hyphens, ≤100 chars including the prefix — so `Data_Platform.01` is refused) is an **error with nothing created**; an account already assigned is `alreadyLinked`, an idempotent no-op that never drives a non-zero exit status; a lost race on workgroup creation re-reads and links to the winner's row, and a lost race on assignment (`DuplicateAccountException`) also reads as `alreadyLinked`, the unique index being the arbiter; duplicate pairs are collapsed before any DB work; names over 255 characters are dropped rather than truncated (a truncated name resolves to a *different* workgroup) and the drop is reported in `errors[]`. When one account carries several names, the correction path uses the most recently updated mapping's — and deliberately leaves the assignment made under the old name in place, because removing one revokes a workgroup's access and a correction run must not do that unasked. Bounded at both ends (§A04): the stored-name scan is paged at the query (`findAwsAccountDisplayNames(Pageable)`, grouped so one account owned by 40 people is one row), `MAX_PAIRS` 20,000 per run and `links[]` capped at 500 with exact counters, and every cap sets `truncated` and logs — never a silent one. §A09: `CREATE_WORKGROUP_FOR_AWS_ACCOUNT` and `LINK_WORKGROUP_ACCOUNT` audit lines carry actor, target and outcome, and every display name reaching a log or an error message goes through `UserMappingService.sanitizeForMessage` (log forging). Fixed while registering the new tool: `list_/add_/remove_workgroup_aws_account` and the three `workgroup_ad_domain` tools were in `McpToolPermissions.LISTING` but **absent from `.CALLING`**, so `tools/call` denied them unconditionally — visible in `tools/list` yet uncallable, the same fail-closed shape as the earlier `add_requirement` and `export_requirements` gaps; a new test pins all seven in both tables and pins `link_workgroup_aws_accounts` to the same permission as `add_workgroup_aws_account`, since the effect is the same. Files with no display name link nothing and report nothing, so every existing Excel and plain-CSV import is byte-identical. Tests: `WorkgroupAccountLinkServiceTest` (19 cases covering the matrix above), `CSVUserMappingParserDisplayNameTest`, `UserMappingCliServiceDisplayNameTest` (including a CSV *without* the column, since commons-csv throws on `get()` for an unknown header), `LinkWorkgroupAwsAccountsToolTest`, plus new cases in `UserMappingBulkImportServiceTest`, `ImportUserMappingsToolTest` and `McpToolPermissionsTest`. Samples: `testdata/user-mappings/accounts-with-display-name.json` and `mappings-with-display-name.csv`, both covering match / create / shared-name / illegal-name in one file. `docs/AWS_ACCOUNT_WORKGROUP_LINKING.md`.

New `product_classification_rule` (ADMIN CRUD, `/admin/product-classification`) drives a materialized `product_class` on `vulnerability`, `installed_product` and `eol_finding`; every list, count, export, statistic and materialized view hides `INSTALLER_ARTIFACT` unless `includeInstallerFindings=true`. Mirrors the proven `excepted` pattern (`VulnQuerySql.VISIBLE`, per-asset recompute at import, chunked full reclassify) and keeps its safe direction — `UNKNOWN` reads as visible. **Rules key on product identity, not path**, because measurement against the live tenant showed the path cannot carry the signal: `Chrome Installer` (222 EOL findings, 17910 rows) returns no path at all, while `C:\Windows\Installer\*.msi` (565594 rows) and `ProgramData\Package Cache\` (150812) are where Windows/WiX keep the package **of an installed product** — treating those as artifacts would have hidden Splunk Universal Forwarder, AWS CLI and Intune. docs/CHANGELOG.md:48:- **AWS account onboarding: welcome mail, direct and guided risk assessments** — the "new AWS account discovered → mail the owner and start an assessment" path becomes a three-mode capability, and the scoping decision moves to the person who actually knows. `WELCOME_ONLY` sends a welcome mail from a classpath template; `DIRECT` additionally starts an assessment for a use case the operator names (today's behaviour); `GUIDED` mails the owner a **one-time, expiring link** whose answers resolve through admin-configured rules into a *set* of use cases, and creates the assessment only on submit, scoped to the **union** of every matching rule. All three run from CLI (`--onboarding-mode`, `--welcome-email`, `--questionnaire-expiry-days` on `import` and `import-s3`), REST and MCP, all dry-runnable, plus a first-class `simulate-onboarding` verb (CLI + REST + MCP `simulate_account_onboarding`) that runs the whole path against a made-up account id and address — the *same* code path a real import runs, not a mock, which is what makes it a rehearsal and why it is rate limited, audited, and stamps every simulated mail with "this is a test, sent by <actor>". **The backward-compatibility contract is the load-bearing part**: a caller sending only `startRiskAssessment=true` — every `extensions/` client, `import-s3`, both existing E2E drivers — resolves to `DIRECT` **with no welcome mail**, byte-identical to before, reconciled in one function (`AccountOnboardingMode.resolve`); an explicit non-`DIRECT` mode combined with that flag is rejected, never guessed. **The matcher never decides**: it sees only choice ids (a BOOLEAN question is two choices, no second code path), every matching active rule contributes and nothing wins, `priorityOrder` is display order only, the single `isDefault` rule is consulted **after** everything else fails, and a resolution producing no requirements in the ACTIVE release is an error rather than an empty questionnaire. Answers that match nothing are **persisted** and the invite stays usable, so an admin can add the missing rule and the owner's original link still works. Rules are normalized tables, not a `ruleJson` blob (`DemandClassificationRule`'s precedent exists for a recursive condition; this one is a flat AND over choice ids, and the rule→use-case link needs real FK integrity). **The public questionnaire is the first genuinely unauthenticated write path in the codebase** and is treated as such: 256-bit `SecureRandom` token (not `UUID.randomUUID()`, because this token *creates* an assessment), single use enforced by a guarded UPDATE **claimed before** creation, 14-day expiry, a byte-identical 404 for malformed/unknown/expired/used/cancelled so the endpoint is no enumeration oracle, the account id **masked** to four digits and the owner email never returned, a new bounded fixed-window rate limiter with a dedicated failed-lookup bucket, `@Secured(IS_ANONYMOUS)` explicit on every method plus an `intercept-url-map` entry so a stale `secman_auth` cookie cannot 401 an owner out of their own link, and the full token never logged, never returned by any API, never printed by the CLI, never in an MCP result and never minted by a dry run — all asserted. Unanswered invites get one reminder then lapse; **nothing is ever auto-created**, because an assessment scoped by a guess looks authoritative and is not. `createAssessment` now takes `useCases: Set<UseCase>` (`use_case_name` widened 255→1024 in V253) and `sendStartNotification` was promoted to `notifyAssessmentStarted` so the guided path reuses the identical mail. Five private helpers were extracted from `AwsAccountRiskAssessmentService` into `EmailTemplateRenderer` — with a **closed template allowlist**, because the basenames are operator config and interpolating one into `getResourceAsStream` would be a classpath-traversal read — and the twice-copied recipient regex into `EmailAddressValidator`. New: ADMIN-**or-SECCHAMPION** admin API and UI (a deliberate widening vs Demand Classification's read-both/write-ADMIN, with a coverage matrix that shows which answer combinations would dead-end *before* an owner hits one), `/onboarding/[token]` public page, `docs/ACCOUNT_ONBOARDING.md` with 28 worked examples covering every mode × dry-run × surface, and the `/account-onboarding` skill in both trees. **OWASP: A01/A02/A03/A04/A05/A07/A08/A09 touched — 0 BLOCK.** **The Kotlin and CLI halves are compile-unverified**: the session had Java 21 only, no Gradle 9.7.0 distribution (services.gradle.org 403s through the agent proxy) and no Maven Central route. The frontend is fully verified — `npm ci`, `npm run build` and 149 unit tests green — as are the skill-sync gate and the driver's bash syntax.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:52:- **`/secure-code` — OWASP Top 10 by construction, with a static gate that is actually tested** — `CLAUDE.md` §"OWASP Top 10 Compliance" was already binding and already good, but it is ~60 bullet points across ten categories, which is more than anyone holds in working memory while writing a controller. The predictable failure is not defiance but **partial recall**: you remember `@Secured` and forget the path id is untrusted; you bind `:name` and forget `ExcelSanitizer` on the export three files over. The new skill closes that gap in three phases. **Phase 1 routes before writing**: a 17-row table maps "does this change accept a client id / write a query / render HTML / take an upload / parse XML / make an outbound call / …" to the two or three A01–A10 categories it can actually violate and, for each, the *one existing control to reuse* — so ten categories collapse to the three that apply, and the answer is a function to call rather than a principle to remember. **Phase 2 writes with that control** (`references/controls.md`: the canonical snippet plus the file that already does it correctly, for all ten categories — `AssetFilterService`, `McpToolGuards`, bound-`:param` queries with a closed allowlist for non-bindables, `DOMPurify` at the assignment site, `ExcelSanitizer`, `ImportController.validateFile`, the `NmapParserService` XXE block, `BCryptPasswordEncoder`, `EncryptedStringConverter`, `SlackClient.validateWebhookUrl`), under three rules: reuse never re-implement, never work around a control to make something build/start/pass, deny by default. **Phase 3 verifies three ways** — the static gate, a semantic re-read against `references/blind-spots.md`, and `/security-review` when the diff touches auth, crypto, upload, export or outbound HTTP — closing with the one-line `OWASP: … touched — clean` verdict the review gate already required. **The gate is `./scripts/owasp-check.sh`**, 27 rules across A01–A10, and its design is mostly a set of decisions about *not* crying wolf. It is **diff-scoped by default** (merge-base with `origin/main`, working tree and **untracked files** included — a freshly generated controller is invisible to `git diff` and is exactly the case this exists for), with two severities: **BLOCK** for a pattern on a line this change added, **REVIEW** for a pre-existing hit in a file you touched. That split is the whole reason the gate is usable: `--all` over the repo reports 101 BLOCK and 1060 REVIEW, and a gate that is red on arrival is a gate everyone learns to ignore. Beyond the greppable rules it does three things a regex alone cannot: it resolves each new `mcp/tools/*.kt` tool name and checks `McpToolPermissions` **LISTING and CALLING separately** (counting names file-wide conflates "listed twice in LISTING" with "listed once in each", and CALLING is additionally fed by a fold over `ToolCategories.CATEGORY_PERMISSIONS`, so checking one file reported 40 of 87 tools as unregistered); it requires an `McpToolGuards` call or an equivalent `context.isAdmin` check, because a missing CALLING entry fails **closed** and looks like a bug someone will chase while a missing guard fails **open** and looks like nothing; and file-context rules (XXE block, upload validation, archive traversal) emit BLOCK only when *this* change introduced the trigger. **Precision was tuned against the real corpus rather than guessed**: the first draft reported 269 BLOCK, of which most were false. "String contains SQL keywords" matches `"Failed to send test email from account: $id"`, so injection rules now require a query-construction context (`@Query(`/`createQuery(`/`nativeQuery`/a string *starting* with SELECT) **and** an interpolation — 24 findings to 1. Naming a secret in a log message is fine (`"using the default password is insecure"`) while logging its *value* is not, so the A09 rule looks for the value reaching the call — `$password`, or a `…Password`/`…Token` identifier passed as an argument — not for the word: 119 to 6, with `len(token)` and `…Configured` explicitly excluded. `A02-secret-lit` no longer fires on `DB_PASSWORD="REDACTED"` (value starting with `$`), and `A08-upload` triggers on a `: CompletedFileUpload` parameter rather than a vestigial import. **`scripts/test/owasp-check-test.sh` is the reason any of that can be trusted.** A static gate fails in two directions and only one is visible: a false positive is loud and gets fixed, a false negative is silent — the rule quietly stops matching and the gate reports OK forever. So the self-test builds a throwaway git repo, plants a deliberately vulnerable fixture per rule, asserts the rule fires **at the right severity**, then plants the repo's *approved* pattern for the same risk (bound `:param`, `DOMPurify.sanitize`, the four XXE `setFeature` calls, `BCryptPasswordEncoder`, a logged `tokenConfigured` boolean) and asserts it stays silent — 30 assertions, all green. It has already earned its keep twice: it caught `\b` in a `file_rule` trigger, which awk does not support, silently downgrading **every** BLOCK to REVIEW and turning the gate green (portable-ERE-only is now documented at the helper), and dogfooding the gate on this very change caught it flagging its own fixtures. Fixed with an exemption that is exactly two paths — `scripts/owasp-check.sh` (it contains the patterns it hunts) and `scripts/test/owasp-check-test.sh` (it is *made of* vulnerable fixtures) — deliberately **not** "tests are exempt", since `CLAUDE.md` forbids a literal credential in "source, tests, scripts or fixtures"; the self-test asserts an ordinary test file still fires, and the exempt paths are printed on every run so the blind spot is visible rather than assumed. **Wiring**: `CLAUDE.md`'s review gate now names the command and the BLOCK/REVIEW contract; `/testsuite` runs the self-test in its fast tier (step 5, "Skill sync and the OWASP gate"); skill registered in both harness trees plus `docs/SKILLS.md`, `docs/SKILLS_AND_AGENTS.md` and `AGENTS.md` (eleven skills → twelve). **Pre-existing findings surfaced by the first audit and left unfixed deliberately** — each encodes a decision that is not this change's to make: `MemoryController` is the only controller with no `@Secured` anywhere (it serves `GET /memory`); 37 MCP tools are in `LISTING` but absent from `CALLING`, including `add_requirement`, `create_release` and `compare_releases`, which per `CLAUDE.md`'s stated rule denies `tools/call` for delegated callers, though the API-key path in `McpToolPermissionService.hasPermission` may still reach them, so the real question is whether the two-map rule or the code is authoritative; `application_register` is absent from both (already documented as intentional); and `WorkgroupAccountsModal.tsx`/`WorkgroupDomainsModal.tsx` still read `localStorage.getItem('authToken')`, dead since the JWT moved to the HttpOnly cookie but exactly the A02 anti-pattern. **OWASP: no category touched** — the change adds two offline shell scripts and Markdown, no endpoint, entity, query or data path; both new scripts are dev tooling that nothing at runtime imports. **Not verified in this environment**: `pass-cli` is unavailable and `SECMAN_HOST` is unset, so the Principle 7 gates (`/e2ejs`, `/e2evulnexception`) did not run; `./gradlew build` and `./scripts/startbackenddev.sh` (Principle 5) were not run either, as no Kotlin, TypeScript or configuration file was changed. `./scripts/check-skill-sync.sh`, `./scripts/test/owasp-check-test.sh` (30/30) and `./scripts/owasp-check.sh` on this branch all pass.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:53:- **AWS account risk assessment: validation pass, three defects closed** — a review of the opt-in auto-start path (`manage-user-mappings import --start-risk-assessment --risk-usecase <name>`, mirrored on `import-s3`, REST `POST /api/user-mappings/bulk` and MCP `import_user_mappings`) confirmed the contract holds — the flag is off by default, the use case comes from a flag, and without the flag the import runs exactly as before — and turned up three things that did not. **(1) The deadline had no upper bound.** `validateStartRequest` rejected `< 1` and nothing else, so `--risk-deadline-days 2147483647` produced an `endDate` outside the SQL `DATE` range; because assessments are started *after* the mapping import commits, that surfaced as a per-account error with the mappings already persisted, and a merely absurd value like `100000` (one keystroke from `1000`) was accepted silently into an assessment the reminder scheduler — which looks two days ahead — would never wake up for. Now `MAX_DEADLINE_DAYS = 3650`, checked in `validateStartRequest` so REST and MCP share it, mirrored as `UserMappingCliService.MAX_RISK_DEADLINE_DAYS` in both CLI commands (the CLI is a separate Gradle module and cannot reference the backend constant; `ImportCommandTest` pins the two together), and clamped rather than thrown in `startAssessmentsForNewAccounts` for a direct service call, since that runs past the commit point. The MCP input schema now advertises `maximum`. **(2) The idempotent skip was reported as a failure.** When a pair already had an open assessment, `createAssessment` returned "an open risk assessment (id=…) already exists" in `AccountRiskAssessmentInfo.error`, so both CLI commands printed it as ❌/FAILED, counted it in `riskAssessmentFailures` and exited 1 — for an outcome that is the feature working correctly. The DTO gained `skipped` / `skipReason` (and the MCP result the same two fields), `error` stays null, and both CLIs render it as a skip that does not affect the exit code. **Load-bearing detail:** the owner-notification gate used to rely on `error != null` to suppress the duplicate mail, so it now tests `!info.skipped` as well — otherwise every re-import would re-notify. The path is only reachable when the mapping row was deleted and the account is imported again while its assessment is still open; a plain re-import never reaches the guard, because the account is no longer new. **(3) The email boundary was too loose.** `UserMappingService.emailRegex` was `^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$`, and `[^@]` matches control characters, spaces and commas — so `alice\r\nBcc: x@evil.com` passed validation. That address is not just a row: it becomes the SMTP recipient of the start and reminder mails, it is interpolated into log lines (`Started risk assessment … owner={}`), and it is written into the assessment's `notes`. The pattern now excludes whitespace and `, ; : < > " \` (a comma makes `InternetAddress.parse` split one recipient into two; a CR/LF reaches a log line), length is capped at the 255-char column width so an overlong address fails as one ordinary row error instead of a post-commit `DataException`, and the three "invalid …" messages that echo the rejected value run it through `sanitizeForMessage` (control characters → `?`, truncated at 80). The same pattern went into `UserMappingBulkImportService`'s `notifyAddress` copy and the CLI's `UserMappingValidator`. Also: `import-s3` now emits the "`--risk-usecase` is ignored because `--start-risk-assessment` is not set" warning `import` already had — silently ignoring it is how an operator ends up believing assessments ran. **Test skill.** `/aws-account-risk-assessment` (driver `scripts/test/test-e2e-aws-account-risk-assessment.sh`) gained three phases: the opt-in default (import a new account with no flag → mapping created, no assessment, no `AWS_ACCOUNT` asset; and the ignored-use-case warning), the deadline bound on both CLI and MCP, and a reworked idempotency phase that actually reaches the guard — it deletes the mapping so the account is new again while the assessment stays open, then asserts exit 0, a "skipped" line, no ❌, and still exactly one tracked assessment. Its **cleanup was also unsafe**: it deleted every risk assessment whose notes contained the substring `886` or `887`, which on a real environment means any assessment for a genuine AWS account whose id contains those digits. It now matches the owner-email prefix the service writes into the notes (`owner: e2e-awsra-`), which is both exact and stable across runs, sweeps mappings by that same prefix instead of this run's two timestamped ids (so earlier interrupted runs are cleaned up too), and finally removes the `AWS_ACCOUNT` basis assets — which nothing removed before, so every run leaked one. Accounts are now one per phase in a fixed `88[4-9]<stamp>000` shape, which is what the asset sweep matches. **Not verified in this session:** the environment had no Gradle distribution and no route to Maven Central, so the Kotlin changes are compile-unverified and neither the unit tests nor the E2E gates were run.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:54:- **Generic chat notifications (Slack + Telegram), configurable per user** — SecMan can now message a user in Slack and/or Telegram when a reportable event completes, with each user choosing their own destination and, independently per channel, which events they want. Two events ship: `CROWDSTRIKE_REPORT_COMPLETED` ("New CrowdStrike report completed") and `AWS_ACCOUNT_IMPORT_COMPLETED` ("New AWS account import completed"). **Architecture is transport- and event-agnostic on purpose.** Publishers know nothing about chat: they publish a `ChatNotificationEvent` (event type, title, summary, label/value fields) and `ChatNotificationEventListener` (`@EventListener @Async`) hands it to `ChatNotificationService`, which resolves subscribers, destinations and rendering. Adding a reportable event is a `NotificationEventType` constant plus one publish call — the settings APIs, both settings UIs and the dispatcher all derive from the enum, so nothing else changes. Adding a transport is one client plus one branch, with no publisher touched. **Subscriptions are rows, not columns**: `user_notification_subscription (user_id, channel, event_type)` — so a new event type or a whole new channel costs no migration, "who wants X over Slack" is a single indexed lookup on the dispatch path, and one user can route CrowdStrike to Slack and AWS imports to Telegram. Saving one channel's settings never disturbs the other's subscriptions (the replace is a per-channel diff, which also preserves `created_at` on kept rows). **Destination resolution.** Slack: personal incoming webhook → the user's channel via the workspace bot → the workspace default channel. Telegram: the user's chat ID is always required (Telegram addresses a conversation, not a person), with the token being the user's personal bot if set, otherwise the workspace bot — so a personal bot keeps working even when workspace delivery is switched off. A subscriber who is enabled but has nowhere to send is recorded as `SKIPPED`, not `FAILED`; the UI resolves the same precedence client-side (`resolveSlackDestination` / `resolveTelegramDestination`) and warns *before* save rather than letting someone tick boxes that silently deliver nothing. **Where the events fire.** AWS account imports complete in one call, so `UserMappingBulkImportService.execute` (REST bulk + MCP, tagged with the calling entry point) and both `ImportController` upload paths publish immediately, after the import has committed and last among the post-commit side effects. CrowdStrike has no such point: a full CLI import arrives as ~94 sub-batch requests across 3 concurrent workers with no well-defined last batch, so `ImportCompletionNotifier` accumulates the run's totals in memory and a `@Scheduled` sweep publishes exactly **one** event once `SECMAN_CHAT_CROWDSTRIKE_QUIET_PERIOD_SECONDS` (180s) have passed with no activity — the same server-side debounce shape, and for the same reason, as `MaterializedViewRefreshService.requestDeferredRefresh`, and it keeps working for older CLI versions, the `/api/crowdstrike/vulnerabilities/save` path and manual callers. **Security.** The per-user Slack webhook URL is the only place in the platform where a non-admin supplies a URL the backend then fetches, so it is checked against a fixed `https://hooks.slack.com/` prefix *and* parsed-host equality (a prefix match alone passes `https://hooks.slack.com.evil.example/...`), rejects userinfo, non-default ports and non-https, and redirects are never followed. The Telegram bot token is interpolated into the request URL **path** (`/bot<token>/sendMessage`), so its `<digits>:<secret>` shape is validated as a security control — a token containing `/` or `..` would otherwise redirect the request to another path on the API host. Slack channels and Telegram chat IDs are validated against conservative character classes. Every credential (both workspace bot tokens, each user's webhook URL and personal bot token) is stored through `EncryptedStringConverter`, never returned by any API — the responses report only `…Configured: true/false` — and the `***HIDDEN***` mask is accepted back to mean "keep the stored value", with `''` meaning "clear it". Slack messages escape Slack's three reserved characters so an imported hostname cannot inject a fake link; Telegram messages are sent with **no** `parse_mode`, deliberately, because MarkdownV2 reserves 18 characters and rejects the whole message on one unescaped occurrence. Every route acts on the caller's own settings — the user id comes from the token and is never read from the body. Dispatch is deliberately **not** `@Transactional`: it performs outbound HTTP with a multi-second timeout per recipient, and wrapping it would pin a pooled DB connection for the whole fan-out (the 2026-07-21 HikariCP starvation incident was exactly that shape). Delivery is per-recipient and per-channel isolated: one bad webhook never stops another user's message, one channel's outage never suppresses the other, and nothing can propagate back into the import that published the event. **New endpoints**: `GET /api/notification-events` (catalogue, authenticated); `GET/PUT /api/slack/settings`, `POST /api/slack/settings/test`, `GET/PUT /api/telegram/settings`, `POST /api/telegram/settings/test` (authenticated, self-scoped); `GET/PUT /api/slack/config`, `POST /api/slack/config/test`, `GET/PUT /api/telegram/config` (ADMIN). No Telegram workspace test endpoint — a bot token addresses no conversation on its own, so a meaningful test needs a chat ID and lives on the user page. **UI**: `/chat-notifications` (all users, linked from the account dropdown) with independent Slack and Telegram cards sharing a `NotificationEventSelector` and `ChatDeliveryStatusLine`; `/admin/chat-config` (ADMIN, linked under System Configuration). **Schema**: `V252__chat_notifications.sql` adds `slack_config`, `telegram_config`, `user_slack_settings`, `user_telegram_settings`, `user_notification_subscription`. **Tests**: `SlackClientTest` and `TelegramClientTest` (the URL/token/channel/chat-id allowlists, including that a rejected value never reaches the network), `ChatMessageRendererTest` (both flavours + Slack escaping), `ChatNotificationServiceTest` (24 cases: subscription filtering, both destination precedence chains, skipped-vs-failed, per-recipient and per-channel isolation, outcome recording), `ImportCompletionNotifierTest` (94 sub-batches → one event with correct totals, nothing published mid-import, totals reset between runs, the account-ID list cap), and `chatValidation.test.ts` on the frontend (17 cases mirroring the backend validators and both destination resolvers). On merging main, the newly-binding §OWASP Top 10 section prompted a re-read of the diff against A01–A10 and turned up one real gap: provider exception text was logged and persisted into `last_delivery_error` verbatim, and several JDK `HttpClient` exceptions echo the request URI — which for Telegram *contains the bot token* and for a Slack webhook *is* the credential. Both clients now scrub the secret out of any error before it is logged or stored (A02: no credential may reach a value that lands in a log), covered by a test per client. Migration renumbered `V251` → `V252__chat_notifications.sql`, since main landed its own `V251__user_profile_picture.sql` — two files sharing a Flyway version fails the migration at boot. **OWASP: A01/A02/A03/A04/A05/A08/A09/A10 touched — clean.** **Not verified in this environment**: `./gradlew build` and `./scripts/startbackenddev.sh` could not run — the session's egress policy blocks `services.gradle.org` and `repo1.maven.org`, and no Gradle 9.7.0 distribution or dependency cache is present — so the backend is compile-unverified and CLAUDE.md principle 5 and the principle-7 E2E gates are undischarged. The frontend gates did run: `npm ci && npm run build` clean, `npm test` 76 passing, and `@astrojs/check` reports zero type errors in any new or changed file (the 10 it finds are all pre-existing in untouched files).
docs/CHANGELOG.md:65:  The section is deliberately **not** generic OWASP advice. Every rule names the control that already exists in this repository, with the instruction to reuse it and never write a second one — and each rule carries the repo-specific failure mode that makes it non-obvious. All named controls were verified against source before being written down, not recalled: **A01** `AssetFilterService.getAccessibleAssets()`/`getAccessibleAssetIds()`/`canAccessAsset(assetId, authentication)` (an id in a request is untrusted input; never `findById(userSuppliedId)` and return it), the restated "SQL pre-filters in materialized views are perf hints, never the auth boundary", and the MCP asymmetry that a missing `McpToolPermissions.CALLING` entry fails *closed* and looks like a bug while a missing `McpToolGuards` check fails **open** and looks like nothing. **A02** `BCryptPasswordEncoder` only, with the SHA-256 path in `McpAuthenticationService` flagged as legacy-migration-only so it is not imitated; JWT stays in the HttpOnly `secman_auth` cookie with the SSE `?token=` param called out as the single documented exception; and the three startup validators (`JwtSigningValidator`, `DatabaseCredentialValidator`, `DatasourceUrlValidator`) marked as fail-the-boot **by design** — never relaxed to make the backend start, which is exactly the pressure a dev hits at 8080. **A03** bound parameters only, naming the ~30 `nativeQuery = true` methods in `VulnerabilityRepository`/`WorkgroupRepository`/`AwsAccountSharingRepository` as the place the rule is easiest to break, plus the allowlist requirement for unbindable fragments (column name, sort direction); `DOMPurify.sanitize(...)` **at the assignment site** per `RichContent.tsx`/`HtmlEditor.tsx`, with the reason sanitize-on-write is insufficient (stored rows predate the control); and `ExcelSanitizer.sanitize()` on every user-controlled export cell, with the note that **no E2E gate ever opens an exported file**, so only `ExcelSanitizerTest` will catch a regression there. **A04** deny-by-default for new endpoints/tools, and "unbounded is a design bug" anchored on the real `findAll()`-then-filter incident that OOM'd `get_vulnerabilities` on 1.1M rows. **A05** do not weaken `SecurityHeadersFilter` (CSP, HSTS, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, COOP/COEP/CORP) — "if a feature *requires* `unsafe-eval`, change the feature"; generic error bodies per `ValidationExceptionHandler`. **A06** pinned versions, `npm ci` as the lockfile gate, and the `src/clinotify` stdlib-only contract. **A07** no bespoke auth paths, and the explicit statement that `X-MCP-User-Email` *identifies* a delegated user but **is not a credential** and must always sit behind a verified API key. **A08** `ImportController.validateFile` as the size/extension/content-type reference, and the four XXE features (`disallow-doctype-decl`, `external-general-entities`, `external-parameter-entities`, `load-external-dtd`) that `NmapParserService` and `MasscanParserService` already set — verified present in both — with "never construct a bare `DocumentBuilderFactory`". **A09** actor+target+outcome logging, and never logging secrets *including at `logger.debug`*, since dev runs with real `pass-cli` secrets loaded. **A10** scheme/host allowlisting for every outbound URL derived from user input or DB config (identity provider endpoints and JWKS, GitHub App, CrowdStrike, S3, webhooks) including cloud metadata `169.254.169.254`, the same check re-applied to redirect targets, and `McpOriginValidationFilter` named as the inbound analogue.
docs/CHANGELOG.md:68:- **Test-coverage evaluation, a repaired frontend test tier, and the `/testsuite` skill** — an audit of what is actually tested here found the frontend tier broken in three independent ways and the fast tier unrepresented in the skill set. **(1) The mandatory frontend gate was unrunnable.** `package-lock.json` had drifted from `package.json` (astro 7.1.3 vs 7.2.0, axios 1.18.1 vs 1.19.0, and 14 more), so CLAUDE.md principle 5a's `npm ci && npm run build` aborted at `npm ci` with `EUSAGE` for everyone, on every checkout — the gate had been passing only for whoever ran `npm install` instead. Lockfile regenerated; `npm ci` → `npm run build` now verified clean. **(2) Eight `*.test.ts` files existed that nothing could run.** No `test` script in `package.json`, no mention in `docs/TESTING.md` (which described "three tiers" and omitted the frontend entirely), no reference in any skill — and two of the eight *failed*: `ProductAutocomplete.test.ts` imported a `.tsx` module (Node's type stripping cannot parse JSX) and `exceptionRequestService.test.ts` died on `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` because the production source imports `'../utils/auth'` extensionless, as Vite resolves but Node does not. Added `npm test` / `npm test:watch` on Node's own runner (no Vitest, no Jest, no new dependency) plus a resolver hook in `src/frontend/test/` (`register.mjs` + `resolve-ts.mjs`) that completes extensionless specifiers to `.ts` — so tests import production modules **as written**, with no production import rewritten for the test runner's benefit — and raises a pointed error naming the extraction convention when a path resolves only to `.tsx`. `getProductSuggestions` extracted from `ProductAutocomplete.tsx` into `productSuggestions.ts`, following the existing `productSearchResults.ts` / `exceptionReviewDto.ts` pattern. docs/CHANGELOG.md:77:  Boxes that legitimately cannot run an agent are handled by a **third, orthogonal exception axis** `kind: ExceptionKind { VULNERABILITY, NO_EDR }` (V247) on both `VulnerabilityException` and `VulnerabilityExceptionRequest` — a *new enum*, not a new `Subject`/`Scope` value, so none of the ~15 exhaustive `when(subject)`/`when(scope)` blocks break and suppression semantics are not inherited. A NO_EDR exception is `scope=ASSET` only, stored with the filler `subject=ALL_VULNS`, **suppresses nothing**, and merely leaves the KPI denominator (reported separately as `excludedByNoEdrException` in the card subtitle). It reuses the entire request → approve/reject/cancel workflow, audit log, SSE badge and expiry scheduler. The "suppresses nothing" invariant is enforced in all three synchronized predicates — `VulnerabilityException.matches()`, `ExceptionMatchSql.EXCEPTION_MATCH` (one leading conjunct, compile-time interpolated into every native site incl. the `recomputeExcepted*` UPDATEs) and `ExceptionMatchIndex` — plus a defence-in-depth filter in `VulnerabilityService.getActiveExceptions()`. **The SQL guard is `(e.kind IS NULL OR e.kind = 'VULNERABILITY')`, not plain equality**: V247 adds the column `NOT NULL DEFAULT` with an explicit backfill, but if a NULL ever occurred (Hibernate `hbm2ddl.auto` creating it where V247 didn't apply, a restored pre-V247 dump) plain equality would stop *every* legacy exception matching and the 03:00 `recomputeAllExceptedScheduled` would clear `excepted` fleet-wide, unattended. The KPI queries use the opposite convention — plain `kind = 'NO_EDR'` — because tolerating NULL there would silently read every legacy exception as an EDR exemption. V247 also **rebuilds `idx_vuln_exception_covering` with `kind` leading**, since V203 created it specifically to keep the correlated `EXCEPTION_MATCH` semi-join index-only. Also updated: `validateInvariants` (NO_EDR branch whose early `return` exempts it from the ADMIN/VULN gate on ALL_VULNS — a normal user must be able to file one, and it is safe because nothing is suppressed), `calculateAffectedCount` → 0, materialization skipped for NO_EDR, `kind` added to the `hasMatchingException`/`deleteExceptionForRequest` identity tuple and the import/export fingerprint (a NO_EDR and a legacy `ALL_VULNS × ASSET` row are otherwise indistinguishable — cancelling one would delete the other), a dedicated `(kind, asset)` duplicate check and supersede branch (the CVE-keyed ones early-return for NO_EDR), and `describeSubject` → "No EDR possible" (unfixed, approval mails read "All Vulnerabilities on host-x"). Entry point: a per-asset **No EDR** action in `AssetManagement.tsx`, shown only when `cloudInstanceId` is set, opening the new `NoEdrExceptionRequestModal` (fixed sentence, no subject/scope pickers); `POST /api/vulnerability-exception-requests` gates `kind=NO_EDR` on `assetFilterService.canAccessAsset`. MCP `create_exception_request` gains `kind` and drops `vulnerabilityId` from `required` (enforced per-kind in the handler, checking `canAccessAsset(assetId)` for NO_EDR); `list_vulnerability_exceptions` and `get_pending_exception_requests` emit and filter it. Tests: `EdrCoverageKpiServiceTest`, `EdrCoverageKpiCountIntegrationTest`, `VulnerabilityExceptionRequestServiceNoEdrTest`, NO_EDR fixtures added to **both** agreement tests (`ExceptionMatchIndexTest`, `ExceptedFlagSqlAgreementIntegrationTest` — which only detect predicate drift if their fixtures contain a NO_EDR row) plus a V247 migration regression asserting a NULL-kind row still suppresses. Docs: `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md`, `docs/MCP.md`.

Each auto-started assessment is *pinned* to it (`lockedRelease` / `isReleaseLocked` / `contentSnapshotTaken` — fields that existed but were never set by anything), and `ResponseController.getRequirementsForAssessment` resolves its questionnaire from that release's `requirement_snapshot` rows scoped by the use case tag, so importing more requirements while the assessment is open cannot change the questions already asked. docs/CHANGELOG.md:95:- **OS + CVE vulnerability exceptions (apply to all assets)** — new exception **scope `OS`** added to the two-axis model (Feature 196). Combined with subject `CVE` it means "these CVEs are excepted on every asset whose `Asset.osVersion` contains the OS string (case-insensitive substring)", e.g. exception OS `Windows Server 2019` also matches `Windows Server 2019 Datacenter`. The OS string is stored in the existing `vulnerability_exception.scope_value` column — **no DB migration** (`scope` is already `VARCHAR(20)`). The match predicate lives in three synchronized places, all updated: the entity `VulnerabilityException.scopeMatches()`, the native-SQL `ExceptionMatchSql.EXCEPTION_MATCH` (`LOCATE(LOWER(scope_value), LOWER(a.os_version)) > 0`, fanning out to ~36 query sites), and the in-memory `ExceptionMatchIndex` in `VulnerabilityService` (which now projects `a.os_version` into `StatusFilteredVulnerabilityRow`). CrowdStrike import is honored automatically: `CrowdStrikeQueryService` computes `hasException` via the shared entity match and `Asset.osVersion` is already populated at import (query-time suppression model — no persistence-time filtering). Also wired through: `validateInvariants`/`createException`/affected-count/`previewExceptionImpact` (new repo methods `count|findByAssetOsVersionContainingIgnoreCase` and `…VulnerabilityIdInAndAssetOsVersionContainingIgnoreCase`), the `/api/vulnerability-exceptions/valid-combinations` matrix (CVE×OS, PRODUCT×OS, ALL_VULNS×OS [ADMIN/VULN]), MCP `create_exception_request` scope enum, and the frontend exception form/table/badges. # SecMan web-security check

`secman-web-check` is the merged command-line scanner for two selectable approaches:
bounded HTTP/TLS security checks and headless-browser visual exposure checks. Run
either approach independently or run both against the same explicit target set.

Redirect chains are reported hop by hop. Cross-host transitions and blocked downgrade,
invalid, or over-limit redirects receive distinct findings.

> Scan only systems you own or are explicitly authorized to assess. Passive scanning is
> the default. Active requests and access to RFC1918/ULA targets require separate,
> explicit opt-ins.

## Five-minute quickstart

Prerequisites: macOS or Linux, Python 3.12 or newer, and
[`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).

```bash
git clone <repository-url> secman_web_check
cd secman_web_check
./scripts/setup.sh
uv run --locked secman-web-check --help
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com \
  --format all \
  --output-dir scan-output \
  --fail-on none
```

Replace `https://example.com` with an authorized target. The final command performs a
passive HTTP/TLS scan and writes terminal, JSON, SARIF, and self-contained HTML output.
Machine reports are placed below `scan-output/` and contain findings only—never raw
response bodies.

You can also activate the virtual environment and use the installed command directly:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
secman-web-check scan https://example.com
```

## Common examples

Select the scan approach explicitly:

```bash
# HTTP/TLS checks only (the backward-compatible default)
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com --scan-mode security

# Browser screenshot plus vision analysis
SECMAN_VISION_API_KEY='REDACTED' \
  uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com --scan-mode visual

# Security and visual scans in one local report
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com \
  --scan-mode both --visual-no-ai --format all --fail-on none
```

`--visual-no-ai` performs deterministic screenshot capture without a model call, so it
cannot report visual-content findings. Screenshots are written below
`OUTPUT_DIR/screenshots` unless `--visual-output-dir` is supplied. Full-page captures
are capped at 4000 pixels.

Scan one public target using safe defaults:

```bash
./scripts/scan-single.sh https://example.com -- --format terminal
```

Verify redirect reporting with the public HTTP testing endpoint:

```bash
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://httpbin.org/redirect/1 \
  --format json \
  --fail-on none
```

The JSON findings include `WEB-TRANSPORT-REDIRECT` for the observed hop. Redirects to a
different hostname, HTTPS downgrades, and blocked redirects receive additional rule IDs.

Scan the example target list and write every format:

```bash
./scripts/scan-list.sh examples/targets.txt -- \
  --config examples/config.toml \
  --format all \
  --output-dir scan-output \
  --fail-on medium
```

Run the documented active probe allowlist:

```bash
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com --active
```

The `--active` flag enables fixed `TRACE`, `OPTIONS`, `.env`, `.git/HEAD`,
`server-status`, and configuration-backup requests. It does not enable crawling,
arbitrary paths, authentication, exploitation, brute force, or fuzzing.

Scan an authorized private target:

```bash
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://10.20.30.40 \
  --allow-private-targets
```

This flag permits only RFC1918 IPv4 and IPv6 ULA addresses. Loopback, link-local,
multicast, unspecified, documentation, and other special-purpose ranges remain denied.
It does not imply `--active`.

## Targets

Supply exactly one positional target, one `--targets-file`, or one `--targets-csv`.
Hostnames without a scheme use HTTPS. Plain target files are UTF-8, one URL or hostname
per line; blank lines and lines beginning with `#` are ignored, and normalized
duplicates are removed.

```bash
secman-web-check scan example.com
secman-web-check scan https://example.com/application/health
secman-web-check scan --targets-file examples/targets.txt
secman-web-check scan --targets-csv testdata/targets-aws.csv
```

AWS target CSV files use this exact header and one account/target pair per row:

```csv
awsAccountNumber,target
111122223333,https://example.com/
444455556666,service.example.org
```

Account numbers must contain exactly 12 digits. The account number is retained in JSON
reports and narrows SecMan subject matching before URI or hostname matching. A normalized
target cannot be assigned to two different accounts in the same file.

User information, URL fragments, non-HTTP schemes, and denied network addresses are
rejected. Every DNS answer and redirect is revalidated. Approved connections pin the
resolved IP while retaining the hostname for HTTP `Host`, TLS SNI, and certificate
verification.

## Reports and exit codes

`--format` is repeatable and accepts `terminal`, `json`, `sarif`, `html`, or `all`.
Terminal is the default. JSON uses schema version `1.0`; SARIF uses version `2.1.0`;
HTML is self-contained, script-free, escaped, and protected by a restrictive CSP.

`--fail-on` accepts `info`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `critical`, or `none` and defaults
to `high`.

- `0`: scan completed and no finding met the configured threshold.
- `1`: at least one finding met the configured threshold.
- `2`: invalid configuration, a failed/partial target, or an operational adapter error.

See [Report formats](docs/REPORTS.md) for schemas and examples.

## Configuration

Configuration precedence is CLI, `SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_*` environment variables, the
`[scan]` table in a TOML file, then safe defaults. The example config keeps active and
private scanning disabled.

```bash
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan --targets-file examples/targets.txt \
  --config examples/config.toml
```

Secrets are never accepted as CLI values or TOML settings. Vision credentials use
`SECMAN_VISION_API_KEY`; optional `SECMAN_VISION_MODEL` and
`SECMAN_VISION_BASE_URL` select the model/provider. See
[Configuration reference](docs/CONFIGURATION.md).

## Optional MariaDB history

MariaDB access occurs only for `db`, `history`, or a scan with `--store-db`.

```bash
export SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_DB_HOST=db.example.invalid
export SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_DB_USER=scanner_user
export SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_DB_PASSWORD='REDACTED'
export SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_DB_NAME=secman_web_check

uv run --locked secman-web-check db install
uv run --locked secman-web-check db status
uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com --store-db
uv run --locked secman-web-check history list --limit 20
```

See [MariaDB setup](docs/DATABASE.md) before applying the example grants.

## Optional SecMan upload

Register separate SecMan scanners for independent lifecycle snapshots: source
`WEB_SECURITY` for security results and source `VISUAL` for visual results. Assign the
same authorized subjects where appropriate. A combined run requires both IDs so one
mode can never resolve findings owned by the other.

```bash
export SECMAN_URL=https://secman.example.invalid
export SECMAN_SECURITY_SCANNER_ID=41
export SECMAN_VISUAL_SCANNER_ID=42
export SECMAN_TOKEN='REDACTED'

uv run --locked secman-web-check scan https://example.com --scan-mode both \
  --format json \
  --push-to-secman
```

Uploads use `/api/integrations/v1`, never fall back to legacy ingestion, and submit each
target as an atomic snapshot. Partial or failed coverage never resolves older findings.
See [SecMan integration](docs/SECMAN.md).

To resolve the SecMan credentials with Proton Pass, copy the reference-only example,
replace its item paths, log in once, and use the wrapper. It always enables direct
SecMan upload:

```bash
cp examples/secman-proton-pass.env .env
${EDITOR:-vi} .env
pass-cli login
./scripts/scan-with-proton-pass.sh \
  --targets-csv testdata/targets-aws.csv \
  --format json \
  --output-dir scan-output \
  --fail-on none
```

Use `--env-file FILE` (or `SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_PASS_ENV_FILE`) for another reference file.
`SECMAN_PASS_CLI` may name a non-default `pass-cli` executable. Resolved secrets remain
in the child process environment and are never added to the scanner command line.
The ready-to-edit CSV used above is stored at `testdata/targets-aws.csv`.

For production on AWS, store the same variables as a JSON object in Secrets Manager
and use the normal AWS credential chain (instance role, task role, or workload
identity). The wrapper allowlists environment keys and never prints the returned
secret:

```bash
./scripts/scan-with-aws-secrets.py \
  --secret-id prod/secman/web-check -- \
  https://example.com --scan-mode both --format json --fail-on none
```

## Development and verification

The repository intentionally keeps Python source files directly under `src/`; the build
maps that directory to the installed `secman_web_check` package.

```bash
./scripts/verify.sh
```

The verification script checks the lockfile, tests, Ruff lint/formatting, strict mypy,
the source distribution, and the wheel. Unit tests use deterministic transports and
mock adapters; they do not require a live target, MariaDB instance, or SecMan deployment.

## Limitations

- No crawling, discovery, authentication testing, exploitation, brute force, or
  arbitrary fuzzing. Visual mode executes the selected page in isolated headless
  Chromium with outbound destination checks on every request.
- Active findings use strong bounded signatures but may still require human validation.
- HTTPS targets use SSLyze for the documented TLS capabilities; unavailable individual
  capabilities make the target partial instead of silently clean.
- MariaDB and SecMan behavior is covered with isolated tests here; operators must verify
  connectivity, permissions, TLS trust, and retention policy in their own environment.
# SecMan REST integration

SecMan upload is disabled unless `--push-to-secman` is supplied. This is the direct
result-import path; no separate export/import step is required.

1. Register a `WEB_SECURITY` scanner for security results and a `VISUAL` scanner for
   visual results.
2. Assign their service users and bind only authorized asset subjects.
3. Set `SECMAN_URL` to the HTTPS origin plus `SECMAN_SECURITY_SCANNER_ID` and/or
   `SECMAN_VISUAL_SCANNER_ID` for the selected modes.
4. Set `SECMAN_TOKEN`, or set `SECMAN_USERNAME` and `SECMAN_PASSWORD`.
5. Run a local JSON report first, then repeat with `--push-to-secman`.

The client discovers subjects through
`GET /api/integrations/v1/scanners/{id}/subjects` and submits atomic target snapshots to
`POST /api/integrations/v1/runs`. Matching prefers the normalized URI and falls back to
the canonical hostname. For `--targets-csv`, the 12-digit AWS account number first
narrows the authorized subject list by `cloudAccountId`, preventing a same-hostname
asset in another account from being selected. Missing or ambiguous matches fail safely.
No inventory is created and no legacy endpoint is attempted.

A complete successful target may resolve older absent findings for that scanner/subject.
Partial and failed results set `completeCoverage=false`, so they never resolve older
findings. Stable external IDs and deterministic run keys make a retry idempotent.

TLS verification is mandatory. Authentication failures and response errors are
sanitized; tokens, passwords, cookies, and raw web response bodies are not uploaded.

Security and visual results intentionally use separate scanner registrations. A
combined run submits two atomic snapshots; the merged local report is not uploaded as
a third snapshot. This prevents a security-only run from resolving visual findings, or
the reverse. `SECMAN_SCANNER_ID` remains a compatibility fallback only for a
single-mode run.

## Proton Pass credentials

The wrapper follows SecMan's `scripts/import.sh` pattern: `pass-cli` resolves references
into a child process environment, then the scanner runs with `--push-to-secman`.

```bash
cp examples/secman-proton-pass.env .env
${EDITOR:-vi} .env
pass-cli login
./scripts/scan-with-proton-pass.sh \
  --targets-csv testdata/targets-aws.csv \
  --format json \
  --output-dir scan-output \
  --fail-on none
```

The reference file must resolve `SECMAN_URL`, the scanner ID(s) required by the chosen
mode, and either
`SECMAN_TOKEN` or the pair `SECMAN_USERNAME` and `SECMAN_PASSWORD`. Do not put resolved
passwords or tokens in the file. Select another file with `--env-file FILE` or
`SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_PASS_ENV_FILE`; select another executable with `SECMAN_PASS_CLI`.

## AWS Secrets Manager credentials

For production, store the required variables in one JSON `SecretString`. Supported
keys are the SecMan URL, scanner IDs, token or username/password, and optional vision
provider settings. Then run:

```bash
./scripts/scan-with-aws-secrets.py --secret-id prod/secman/web-check -- \
  https://example.com --scan-mode both --format json --fail-on none
```

The script relies on the standard AWS CLI credential chain, rejects unknown JSON keys,
does not echo the secret response, and passes resolved values only in the child process
environment.

## AWS target CSV

`--targets-csv` accepts UTF-8 CSV with this exact header:

```csv
awsAccountNumber,target
111122223333,https://example.com/
444455556666,service.example.org
```

Each account number must be exactly 12 digits and each target must pass the normal URL
and network-policy validation. Blank targets, unexpected columns, malformed rows, and
the same normalized target assigned to different accounts are rejected before scanning.
The account is included in the JSON report and in the SecMan subject-selection step.
A ready-to-edit example is available at `testdata/targets-aws.csv`.
# MariaDB history

Persistence is disabled unless the operator invokes a database/history command or uses
`--store-db`. MariaDB is the only supported database backend.

1. Review [the example grants](../db/grants.example.sql) and replace every placeholder.
2. Create the database/user with an administrative account outside this tool.
3. Export the scanner's least-privilege connection variables described in
   [CONFIGURATION.md](CONFIGURATION.md).
4. Run `./scripts/install-db.sh`, then `secman-web-check db status`.
5. Add `--store-db` only to scans whose history should be retained.

The schema stores version/checksum metadata, scan runs, explicit targets, normalized
findings, completeness, and sanitized errors. All target-controlled values use DB-API
parameters. A run write is transactional; a failure rolls it back and returns exit code
2 without removing reports already generated on disk.

Use a trusted CA with `SECMAN_WEB_CHECK_DB_SSL_CA` when the database requires TLS. The
scanner never prints or persists the database password.
