- **AWS account risk assessment: validation pass, three defects closed** — a review of the opt-in auto-start path (`manage-user-mappings import --start-risk-assessment --risk-usecase <name>`, mirrored on `import-s3`, REST `POST /api/user-mappings/bulk` and MCP `import_user_mappings`) confirmed the contract holds — the flag is off by default, the use case comes from a flag, and without the flag the import runs exactly as before — and turned up three things that did not. **(1) The deadline had no upper bound.** `validateStartRequest` rejected `< 1` and nothing else, so `--risk-deadline-days 2147483647` produced an `endDate` outside the SQL `DATE` range; because assessments are started *after* the mapping import commits, that surfaced as a per-account error with the mappings already persisted, and a merely absurd value like `100000` (one keystroke from `1000`) was accepted silently into an assessment the reminder scheduler — which looks two days ahead — would never wake up for. Now `MAX_DEADLINE_DAYS = 3650`, checked in `validateStartRequest` so REST and MCP share it, mirrored as `UserMappingCliService.MAX_RISK_DEADLINE_DAYS` in both CLI commands (the CLI is a separate Gradle module and cannot reference the backend constant; `ImportCommandTest` pins the two together), and clamped rather than thrown in `startAssessmentsForNewAccounts` for a direct service call, since that runs past the commit point. The MCP input schema now advertises `maximum`. **(2) The idempotent skip was reported as a failure.** When a pair already had an open assessment, `createAssessment` returned "an open risk assessment (id=…) already exists" in `AccountRiskAssessmentInfo.error`, so both CLI commands printed it as ❌/FAILED, counted it in `riskAssessmentFailures` and exited 1 — for an outcome that is the feature working correctly. The DTO gained `skipped` / `skipReason` (and the MCP result the same two fields), `error` stays null, and both CLIs render it as a skip that does not affect the exit code. **Load-bearing detail:** the owner-notification gate used to rely on `error != null` to suppress the duplicate mail, so it now tests `!info.skipped` as well — otherwise every re-import would re-notify. The path is only reachable when the mapping row was deleted and the account is imported again while its assessment is still open; a plain re-import never reaches the guard, because the account is no longer new. **(3) The email boundary was too loose.** `UserMappingService.emailRegex` was `^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$`, and `[^@]` matches control characters, spaces and commas — so `alice\r\nBcc: x@evil.com` passed validation. That address is not just a row: it becomes the SMTP recipient of the start and reminder mails, it is interpolated into log lines (`Started risk assessment … owner={}`), and it is written into the assessment's `notes`. The pattern now excludes whitespace and `, ; : < > " \` (a comma makes `InternetAddress.parse` split one recipient into two; a CR/LF reaches a log line), length is capped at the 255-char column width so an overlong address fails as one ordinary row error instead of a post-commit `DataException`, and the three "invalid …" messages that echo the rejected value run it through `sanitizeForMessage` (control characters → `?`, truncated at 80). The same pattern went into `UserMappingBulkImportService`'s `notifyAddress` copy and the CLI's `UserMappingValidator`. Also: `import-s3` now emits the "`--risk-usecase` is ignored because `--start-risk-assessment` is not set" warning `import` already had — silently ignoring it is how an operator ends up believing assessments ran. **Test skill.** `/aws-account-risk-assessment` (driver `scripts/test/test-e2e-aws-account-risk-assessment.sh`) gained three phases: the opt-in default (import a new account with no flag → mapping created, no assessment, no `AWS_ACCOUNT` asset; and the ignored-use-case warning), the deadline bound on both CLI and MCP, and a reworked idempotency phase that actually reaches the guard — it deletes the mapping so the account is new again while the assessment stays open, then asserts exit 0, a "skipped" line, no ❌, and still exactly one tracked assessment. Its **cleanup was also unsafe**: it deleted every risk assessment whose notes contained the substring `886` or `887`, which on a real environment means any assessment for a genuine AWS account whose id contains those digits. It now matches the owner-email prefix the service writes into the notes (`owner: e2e-awsra-`), which is both exact and stable across runs, sweeps mappings by that same prefix instead of this run's two timestamped ids (so earlier interrupted runs are cleaned up too), and finally removes the `AWS_ACCOUNT` basis assets — which nothing removed before, so every run leaked one. Accounts are now one per phase in a fixed `88[4-9]<stamp>000` shape, which is what the asset sweep matches. **Not verified in this session:** the environment had no Gradle distribution and no route to Maven Central, so the Kotlin changes are compile-unverified and neither the unit tests nor the E2E gates were run.
- **Generic chat notifications (Slack + Telegram), configurable per user** — SecMan can now message a user in Slack and/or Telegram when a reportable event completes, with each user choosing their own destination and, independently per channel, which events they want. Two events ship: `CROWDSTRIKE_REPORT_COMPLETED` ("New CrowdStrike report completed") and `AWS_ACCOUNT_IMPORT_COMPLETED` ("New AWS account import completed"). **Architecture is transport- and event-agnostic on purpose.** Publishers know nothing about chat: they…11464 tokens truncated…limit=10` (backing a new `/account-finding-age` page plus an ADMIN-only card on the home dashboard), MCP `get_top_accounts_by_finding_age` (ADMIN via delegation, `VULNERABILITIES_READ`), and CLI `send-account-finding-age-report` which emails the table to all ADMIN-role users (deliberately excluding REPORT users). Every row carries an account name: the new `aws_account` table (V245) holds admin-supplied names, edited inline on the report page via `PUT /api/admin/aws-accounts/{id}/name`, and unnamed accounts fall back to their bare 12-digit ID. Docs: `docs/CLI.md`, `docs/MCP.md`.

- **Vulnerability exception expiry reminders** — CLI `send-exception-expiry-reminders` / MCP `send_exception_expiry_reminders` (ADMIN, `NOTIFICATIONS_SEND`) notify exception owners when their `VulnerabilityException` is expiring exactly `--days`/`days` days from today (default **7**). Owner = the exception's `createdBy` username resolved to `User.email`; one consolidated email per owner listing all of their expiring exceptions. Sent-state table `vulnerability_exception_expiry_reminder` (V244, `VulnerabilityExceptionExpiryReminder`, unique on `(exception_id, expiration_date)`) makes the reminder idempotent per (exception, expiration date) pair — safe to run daily via cron without re-notifying, while editing an exception to a new expiration date triggers a fresh reminder once it re-enters the window. Backend: `VulnerabilityExceptionExpiryReminderService`, endpoint `POST /api/cli/vulnerability-exception-expiry-notifications/send` (ADMIN). No scheduler — CLI/MCP-triggered only, matching `send-patch-notifications`/`notify-new-accounts`; both `./scripts/secman` (Proton Pass) and `./scripts/secmancliaws.sh` (AWS Secrets Manager) dispatch the new subcommand via the existing generic CLI launchers — no new wrapper scripts needed. Docs: `docs/CLI.md`, `docs/MCP.md`.

- **Role-based home dashboard** — after login, users **without** ADMIN or SECCHAMPION get a personal "My Tasks" dashboard on `/` instead of the platform statistics view (ADMIN/SECCHAMPION keep `HomeStatisticsDashboard`; switch in `HomeDashboard.tsx`, mount-gated to stay hydration-safe). Backend: one aggregated `GET /api/user-dashboard` (IS_AUTHENTICATED, `UserDashboardController`/`UserDashboardService`) returns accessible-asset count, open vuln severity counts (reuses `findSeverityDistributionForAssets`, exception-filtered), an overdue-patching summary (new single-row native aggregates `aggregateOverdueForAssets`/`aggregateOverdueForAll` on the outdated-asset materialized view — accessible-ID filter is the auth boundary), the user's own exception-request counts (`getUserRequestSummary`), open risk assessments where the user is the **respondent** (soonest deadline first, capped at 10, `/respond/{token}` link when a valid unused `AssessmentToken` exists), and view flags (AWS account / workgroup / domain vulns) for quick links. Accessible-asset IDs resolve once per request via `AccessibleAssetIdsCache`; ADMIN/SECCHAMPION callers get unscoped query variants so no giant IN clause is ever built. Frontend: `UserTodoDashboard.tsx` renders the whole page from that one response (KPI tiles, "Action required" list, "Waiting on others", "Your views"). Unit coverage: `UserDashboardServiceTest`.

- **AWS clean-server security KPI on the dashboard** — post-login dashboard (`HomeStatisticsDashboard.tsx`) now shows, for **ADMIN and SECCHAMPION** users only, the percentage of AWS servers with **no vulnerability older than 30 days** (fixed window, independent of the admin-tunable `VulnerabilityConfig.reminderOneDays` overdue-reminder threshold). "AWS server" = an asset with a non-blank `cloudInstanceId` (same definition as `AssetRepository.countAllAwsAssetsWithInstanceId`, used by asset-match-clear), which naturally excludes the synthetic `AWS_ACCOUNT` placeholder assets. Always precomputed — `GET /api/dashboard/aws-clean-server-kpi` (ADMIN/SECCHAMPION) only ever reads a cached value, never queries live, so login stays fast regardless of fleet size. `AwsCleanServerKpiService.recalculate()` runs inside `MaterializedViewRefreshService.refreshDerivedData()` (same non-fatal try/catch pattern as the statistics cache and heatmap refreshes there), so the KPI is recomputed after every CrowdStrike import and every manual admin materialized-view refresh, honoring active vulnerability exceptions the same way the outdated-assets view does. Persisted by reusing the existing `vulnerability_statistics_cache` table (`cache_key = "aws_clean_server_kpi"`, no new schema). Before the first calculation ever completes, the dashboard shows **"Not available"**.

- **GitHub / Dependabot Alerts consolidation** — the standalone Vulnerability Management → "Dependabot alerts" page is retired; its one unique capability (raw per-alert detail: package, CVE/GHSA, vulnerable range, patched version) is folded into the "GitHub" view (`/github-repos`) as expandable per-repo rows. `GithubRepoImportService` now also persists `GithubRepoDependabotAlert` rows (new `github_repo_dependabot_alert` table, V239) — current-state only, deleted and reinserted per repo on every import (same pattern as the CrowdStrike vulnerability import). New endpoint `GET /api/github/repositories/{id}/alerts` (ADMIN/VULN/SECCHAMPION). Removed: the `dependabot_alert` table (dropped by V239), `DependabotAlertController`/`Service`/`Repository`/entity, the CLI `query dependabot-alerts` command (PAT-based GitHub auth is no longer used anywhere — GitHub App auth is now the sole ingestion path), and the "Dependabot alerts" sidebar entry. Docs: `docs/GITHUB_REPOS.md` (`docs/DEPENDABOT.md` removed).

- **GitHub repository vulnerability management** (V238) — inventory of all repos accessible via a **GitHub App** (credentials on the new ADMIN dashboard `/admin/github-config`, `POST/GET/PUT/DELETE /api/github-config` + `/{id}/test`; private key encrypted via `EncryptedStringConverter`, masked `***HIDDEN***`). New **Vulnerability Management → GitHub** view (`/github-repos`, ADMIN/VULN/SECCHAMPION) shows name, owner, open **critical/high** Dependabot alert counts, last import, last high/critical finding, editable per-repo `ownerEmail` and exception badge. Import (`POST /api/github/import`, ADMIN/VULN; CLI `import-github-repos`; MCP `import_github_repos` [ADMIN/VULN, `VULNERABILITIES_READ`]) runs **server-side** GitHub App calls (RS256 App JWT via `util/PemUtils` — PKCS#1+PKCS#8, plain JDK crypto → installation token → paginated repo + alert queries in `GithubAppClientService`), upserts `github_repository` by stable numeric repo id and writes one `github_repo_finding_snapshot` per repo per run. **30-day non-decrease alert** (`POST /api/cli/github-repo-alerts/send`, ADMIN; CLI `alert-github-repo-owners --days --dry-run`; MCP `send_github_repo_alerts` [ADMIN, `NOTIFICATIONS_SEND`]): baseline = newest snapshot ≥ N days old, alert when current high+critical `> 0` and `>=` baseline, one email per `ownerEmail` (template `github-repo-alert.{html,txt}`); repos with an active `github_repo_alert_exception` (reason, optional expiry; managed in the GitHub view, ADMIN/VULN) are skipped, no-email repos reported as `unmappedRepos`, young repos as `reposSkippedInsufficientHistory`. Pure DB operation — no GitHub call at alert time. E2E: Phase 8d in `scripts/test/test-e2e-vuln-exception-full.sh` (`RUN_PHASE8D`/`--skip-phase8d`). Docs: `docs/GITHUB_REPOS.md`, `docs/CLI.md`, `docs/MCP.md`.

- **CLI `manage-user-mappings import --start-risk-assessment`** — the mapping import (also `import-s3`) can auto-start a risk assessment for the owner of every **brand-new AWS account** it introduces. All parameters come from the command line: `--risk-usecase <name>` (mandatory with the flag; must name an existing use case, case-insensitive) and `--risk-deadline-days <n>` (default **7**, min 1). The **assessor is any user with the SECCHAMPION role** (round-robin over all SECCHAMPIONs); validation fails fast (400/exit 2) when the use case is unknown or no SECCHAMPION exists. Per (new account, owner email) pair: an `AWS_ACCOUNT` asset (`AWS Account <id>`, `cloudAccountId` set, owner = email) is found-or-created, an ASSET-based `RiskAssessment` (status STARTED, endDate = today + deadline, respondent = owner user when one exists) is created **after** the import commits, and the owner is emailed. **Reminders 2 days and 1 day before the deadline** are sent by `AwsAccountRiskAssessmentReminderScheduler` (daily 08:15) to the owner; sent-state persists on the new `aws_account_risk_assessment` table (V237, `AwsAccountRiskAssessment` entity) so each reminder fires exactly once and only import-created assessments are reminded (missed 2-day reminders collapse into the 1-day send). Backend: `AwsAccountRiskAssessmentService`, new fields on `POST /api/user-mappings/bulk` (`startRiskAssessment`, `riskAssessmentUseCase`, `riskAssessmentDeadlineDays`) with `riskAssessments[]` in the response. Docs: `docs/CLI.md`.

- **OS + CVE vulnerability exceptions (apply to all assets)** — new exception **scope `OS`** added to the two-axis model (Feature 196). Combined with subject `CVE` it means "these CVEs are excepted on every asset whose `Asset.osVersion` contains the OS string (case-insensitive substring)", e.g. exception OS `Windows Server 2019` also matches `Windows Server 2019 Datacenter`. The OS string is stored in the existing `vulnerability_exception.scope_value` column — **no DB migration** (`scope` is already `VARCHAR(20)`). The match predicate lives in three synchronized places, all updated: the entity `VulnerabilityException.scopeMatches()`, the native-SQL `ExceptionMatchSql.EXCEPTION_MATCH` (`LOCATE(LOWER(scope_value), LOWER(a.os_version)) > 0`, fanning out to ~36 query sites), and the in-memory `ExceptionMatchIndex` in `VulnerabilityService` (which now projects `a.os_version` into `StatusFilteredVulnerabilityRow`). CrowdStrike import is honored automatically: `CrowdStrikeQueryService` computes `hasException` via the shared entity match and `Asset.osVersion` is already populated at import (query-time suppression model — no persistence-time filtering). Also wired through: `validateInvariants`/`createException`/affected-count/`previewExceptionImpact` (new repo methods `count|findByAssetOsVersionContainingIgnoreCase` and `…VulnerabilityIdInAndAssetOsVersionContainingIgnoreCase`), the `/api/vulnerability-exceptions/valid-combinations` matrix (CVE×OS, PRODUCT×OS, ALL_VULNS×OS [ADMIN/VULN]), MCP `create_exception_request` scope enum, and the frontend exception form/table/badges. Docs: `docs/MCP.md`. **Request path completed**: the per-vulnerability "Request Exception" modal (`ExceptionRequestModal.tsx`) now offers an OS scope card (CVE×OS, free-text OS substring input), the MCP `list_vulnerability_exceptions` scope filter accepts `OS`, and the E2E subject×scope matrix in `scripts/test/test-e2e-vuln-exception-full.sh` Phase 8c covers all 5 scopes (28 fixtures: 2 actions × (3×5 − forbidden `ALL_VULNS×GLOBAL`); OS cases seed `asset.os_version` via SQL with case-differing substring scope values). Unit coverage: `VulnerabilityExceptionRequestServiceOsScopeTest`, `ListVulnerabilityExceptionsToolTest`.

- **Operating system per CrowdStrike asset** — the `query servers --save` import now captures each host's OS and stores it on `Asset.osVersion` (no separate command, no extra CrowdStrike round-trip). OS is extracted in `CrowdStrikeApiClientImpl.mapResponseToDtos` (shared) from the device entity (`os_version`, fallback `platform_name`, then `host_info.os_version`/`platform`) and carried on `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityDto.osVersion` → `ServerVulnerabilityBatch.osVersion` (latest-detected non-blank per host) → `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityBatchDto.osVersion`. Backend persistence (`createNewAsset`/`updateAsset`) was already in place. Now also exposed read-only on `GET /api/assets` (`AssetResponse.osVersion`, intentionally reversing part of HI-8) and shown as the **OS** column in the asset management UI. Docs: `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md`.

- **`send-notification-users` recipient fan-out** — the global vulnerability-notification flow (also reused by `send-patch-notifications`) now notifies, for each affected AWS account, the union of: (1) the account owner(s) via `UserMapping.findByAwsAccountId`, (2) members of any workgroup containing an EC2 asset in the account (`AssetRepository.REDACTED`, asset→workgroup→users), and (3) users granted access via the sharing feature (`AwsAccountSharingRepository.findTargetUserEmailsByAwsAccountId`, the inverse of the access-control query, honoring per-rule account selection). Recipients are deduplicated case-insensitively; an account with zero recipients across all three paths is reported as unmapped. Logic in `UserVulnerabilityNotificationService.resolveAccountRecipients`. Docs: `docs/CLI.md`.

- **CLI `notify-new-accounts`** — notifies users about new AWS account mappings created within a configurable look-back window (default: 24 h). Queries `UserMapping` rows where `aws_account_id IS NOT NULL AND created_at >= now() - hours` (new `UserMappingRepository.findRecentAwsAccountMappings`), groups by email, and sends one consolidated email per user. The notification body text is read from a file supplied via `--file`/`-f` (mandatory) — operators customise the message without redeploying. The account list is always appended below the custom text. New `NewAccountNotificationService` follows the same pattern as `UserVulnerabilityNotificationService`. Backend endpoint: `POST /api/cli/new-account-notifications/send` (ADMIN). Docs: `docs/CLI.md`.

- **CLI `send-patch-notifications` + MCP `send_patch_notifications`** — notify users about missing patches (overdue vulnerabilities), batched by the **first character of their email** (mandatory positional arg, e.g. `a`). `--days` (default 30) and `--dry-run` optional. Reuses `UserVulnerabilityNotificationService.sendUserVulnerabilityNotifications` (new `emailPrefix` recipient filter — case-insensitive `startsWith`, applied after AWS-account→user mapping) and the existing `POST /api/cli/user-vulnerability-notifications/send` endpoint (new optional `emailPrefix` field). MCP tool is ADMIN-only via delegation, permission `NOTIFICATIONS_SEND`. E2E coverage: Phase 8b in `scripts/test/test-e2e-vuln-exception-full.sh` (dry-run + missing-arg + non-admin negatives). Docs: `docs/CLI.md`, `docs/MCP.md`.

- **Feature 088** — AI-assisted risk-assessment answers (V215, V216). ADMIN and SECCHAMPION users (the assessment's assessor or requestor; ADMIN can act on any) can trigger an OpenRouter LLM to pre-fill compliance answers as draft `Response` rows with confidence + citations. Human always reviews and submits.
  - DB-backed master switch on `app_settings.ai_risk_assessment_enabled` (V216), flippable by ADMIN at `/appsettings`. Env var `AI_RISK_ASSESSMENT_ENABLED` only seeds the default at first create — once a row exists, the DB column is authoritative. `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` resolved via `pass-cli` is still required for the feature to actually call out. The UI "AI Pre-fill" button is gated on `GET /api/ai-risk-assessment/status` so it stays hidden when the switch is off.
  - Per-job hard cost cap `secman.ai.risk-assessment.max-cost-per-job-usd` (default 5 USD) plus global concurrency cap `max-concurrent-jobs-global` (default 2). Pre-flight rejects over-budget runs; mid-flight aborts and marks `FAILED`, retaining partial successes.
  - New endpoints under `/api/risk-assessments/{id}/ai-suggestions/...`: `POST /jobs`, `GET /jobs/{jobId}`, `DELETE /jobs/{jobId}` (cancel), `GET /jobs/{jobId}/events` (SSE), `GET` (list applied), `POST /clear-low-confidence`. All `@Secured("ADMIN","SECCHAMPION")` plus `AssessmentOwnershipGuard`.
  - Provenance: new `response.source` column (`MANUAL | AI_GENERATED | AI_EDITED`, indexed, backfilled `MANUAL`) plus `response.ai_suggestion_id` FK. `ResponseController` flips `AI_GENERATED → AI_EDITED` whenever a human changes answerType or comment.
  - Confidence band derivation: `score = 0.5·self_reported + 0.3·min(valid_citations, 3)/3 + 0.2·answer_is_not_UNKNOWN`. HIGH requires ≥1 valid citation (downgrade rule). Stored both raw + band so thresholds can retune without re-running the model.
  - Redaction (NFR-4): `PromptBuilder.redact()` scrubs emails, IPv4 addresses, and `*.internal/*.local/*.corp/*.lan/*.intranet` URLs from the prompt regardless of caller hygiene. Locked by `PromptBuilderTest`.
  - Re-run safety: `startJob` excludes `source = AI_EDITED` rows unless `force = true`. `clear-low-confidence` only touches `AI_GENERATED` rows whose linked suggestion has `confidenceBand = LOW`.
  - Mirrors `TranslationService` (JDK HttpClient + dedicated `ai` executor + Caffeine 24h cache) and `ExportJobService` (DB-backed job, IO executor, heartbeat, scheduled stale-job reclaim).
  - Docs: `docs/AI_RISK_ASSESSMENT.md`; spec/plan/tasks under `specs/088-ai-risk-assessment-answers/`.



- **CLI `asset-match-clear`** — reconciles AWS assets against an authoritative resource snapshot JSON downloaded from S3. Required env vars `AWS_ASSET_BUCKET_NAME` and `AWS_ASSET_BUCKET_KEY_NAME` (or `--bucket`/`--key`). Matches `Asset.cloudInstanceId` (case-insensitive) against the snapshot's `resourceId` set, scoped strictly to `accountId`s present in the snapshot — assets in other accounts are never touched (partial-snapshot safe). Default safety brake at 25% (`--max-delete-percent`, set 0 to disable); empty snapshots are rejected. Backend endpoint: `POST /api/assets/match-clear-aws` (ADMIN). Full reference: `docs/CLI_ASSET_MATCH_CLEAR.md`.

- **CrowdStrike stale-vuln cleanup hardening** (V213, V214). Closes the silent-remediation gap when a host's only matching vulnerability gets patched and it drops out of the next CLI batch:
  - `vulnerability.source` column (V213) replaces owner-based scoping in the reconcile sweep — CrowdStrike vulns on human-owned assets are now cleaned up. Canonical literals: `com.secman.constants.VulnerabilitySources` (`CROWDSTRIKE`, `XLSX`, `CLI_MANUAL`, `UNKNOWN`).
  - `crowdstrike_severity_history` table (V214) persists the union of all severities ever queried; the reconcile sweeps that union, not just today's `--severity` flag. Drift across runs no longer leaves stale rows.
  - CLI hard-fails (exit 2) on reconcile HTTP errors via `ReconcileFailedException` — operators/cron see the failure instead of a silent warning.
  - Repository method renamed: `VulnerabilityRepository.deleteStaleCrowdStrikeImports` → `deleteStaleVulnerabilitiesBySource`.
  - Coverage: `CrowdStrikeStaleVulnerabilityIntegrationTest` (5 cases).

- **Feature 087** — CrowdStrike legacy stale-asset cleanup. Adds rule B alongside the existing timestamp rule:
  - Canonical owner literal lives at `com.secman.constants.AssetOwners.CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT`. Used as the writer in `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityImportService.createNewAsset`, the dropdown source in `AssetController.getOwnerCandidates`, and the predicate parameter for `AssetRepository.findLegacyCrowdStrikeStale`.
  - New flag `secman.crowdstrike.cleanup.include-legacy` (env: `CROWDSTRIKE_CLEANUP_INCLUDE_LEGACY`, default `false`) gates rule B. Manual runs may override per-call via `includeLegacy: Boolean?` on the request body.
  - Rule-B fence: `owner = "CrowdStrike Import"` AND `crowdStrikeLastImportedAt IS NULL` AND no `manualCreator` AND no `scanUploader` AND `COALESCE(lastSeen, updatedAt, createdAt) < cutoff`.
  - `crowdstrike_cleanup_run` gains `legacy_candidate_count` and `legacy_deleted_count` (V210). Safety brake denominator widens to `countCrowdStrikeTracked + countLegacyCrowdStrikeTotal` when `include-legacy` is on.
  - Each cleanup candidate carries a `CleanupCandidateReason` enum (`TIMESTAMP_STALE` | `LEGACY_NULL_TIMESTAMP`) — surfaced in the dry-run summary and history table on the admin Falcon-config page.

# Changelog (archived from CLAUDE.md)

## Context summaries preserved before compression (2026-09-06)

- **Source-review quick wins: hot-path queries, transaction scope, dashboard parallelism (2026-08-27)** — first execution pass over `docs/SOURCE_REVIEW_COMPLEXITY_SPEED.md` §6. `AssetFilterService` admin paths use a new `findAllIds()` projection and the scan path became two batch queries (no more full-table `findAll()` + in-memory filter); eight `findAll().filter{hasRole}` sites became role queries; `NormMappingService` no longer holds a transaction across its OpenRouter loop (per-requirement apply transactions via self-`Provider`); the private CrowdStrike deadlock-retry copy merged into shared `DeadlockRetry`; new `GET /api/workgroups/tree` replaces the frontend's recursive per-node walk; home dashboard fetches run concurrently, the `McpDashboard` interval leak is fixed, dead `utils/api-config.ts` and the legacy unpaged `getCurrentVulnerabilities` are deleted. Backend build/startup + E2E gates still owed before merge (authoring env had no Gradle mirror/DB/pass-cli) — detail in `docs/CHANGELOG.md`.

- **AWS account display names link accounts to workgroups (2026-08-25)** — an account whose `display_name` is `DevOps-x` now belongs to workgroup **`aws-DevOps-x`**: matched exactly (case-insensitively) on the `aws-` prefix, **created** when missing. One implementation, `WorkgroupAccountLinkService`, reached from the import (CLI/REST/MCP `displayName`, after the mappings commit) and from a correction path that re-links from stored names with no file — CLI `manage-user-mappings link-workgroups`, `POST /api/user-mappings/link-workgroup-accounts`, MCP `link_workgroup_aws_accounts`. The name is persisted as `user_mapping.aws_account_name` (V260) and deliberately kept **out** of the unique key. A display name that cannot be a workgroup name is an error row, never a forced creation; already-linked accounts are idempotent no-ops. Also fixed: six workgroup MCP tools were in `LISTING` but not `.CALLING` (listed yet uncallable). `docs/AWS_ACCOUNT_WORKGROUP_LINKING.md`.

- **Full `excepted` recompute chunked to stop multi-minute lock holds (2026-08-24)** — `recomputeExceptedAll()` was one `UPDATE` with **no WHERE**, locking every `vulnerability` row (~1.8M) plus `vulnerability_exception` for 53-180s, so every concurrent writer (bulk exception delete/import, CrowdStrike import, per-asset recompute) queued behind it. `AsyncExceptionRecompute.recomputeAllChunked` now drives bounded **keyset** chunks (`CHUNK_SIZE` 10,000) through `recomputeExceptedForIdRange`, each its own REQUIRES_NEW transaction with per-chunk `DeadlockRetry`. Atomicity is deliberately given up (the path is already `@Async` and eventual); a failure now leaves a converged prefix. `recomputeExceptedAll()` is retained for integration tests only. `docs/CHANGELOG.md`.

## Full change entries

- **Full `excepted` recompute chunked to stop multi-minute lock holds (2026-08-24)** — `VulnerabilityRepository.recomputeExceptedAll()` was a single `UPDATE vulnerability v JOIN asset a … SET v.excepted = CASE WHEN EXISTS(…)` **with no WHERE clause**. It took exclusive row locks on every `vulnerability` row (~1.8M in production) and, through its correlated subquery, read locks on `vulnerability_exception` — holding both for the entire 53–180s transaction. Every concurrent writer to either table then blocked until lock-wait-timeout: bulk exception delete/import, CrowdStrike imports, per-asset recomputes. `DeadlockRetry` absorbed the failure, which is exactly why it stayed hidden — but the *other* operation still paid the full timeout first, observed as ~40s per `delete_all_vulnerability_exceptions` in both E2E runs, contending with "Async full excepted recompute complete: 1824736 rows in 53481 ms". Fix: `AsyncExceptionRecompute.recomputeAllChunked` drives the recompute as bounded **keyset** chunks (`CHUNK_SIZE` 10,000) through the new `recomputeExceptedForIdRange(afterId, throughId)`, each in its own REQUIRES_NEW transaction with per-chunk `DeadlockRetry`. Lock hold per transaction drops from minutes to milliseconds, so competing writers interleave between chunks instead of queueing behind one lock set; a chunk that loses a race replays only its own id range instead of the whole statement. **Keyset, not fixed-width id stepping** — the CrowdStrike import is delete-then-insert per asset, so ids are sparse and `MAX(id)` runs far ahead of the row count, which would make blind stepping spend most iterations on empty ranges. The daily 03:00 `recomputeAllExceptedScheduled` now delegates to the same driver (its orphaned `selfProvider` removed), so the nightly pass stops reintroducing the hold. Chunking gives up atomicity, and that is argued rather than assumed: the operation is already `@Async`, its documented contract is already eventual ("rows stay visible until it lands", failures "non-fatal; standing sweeps will retry"), a mid-statement failure already left partial state, and readers evaluate `v.excepted = 0` per row without a cross-table snapshot — so no guarantee is lost, and a failure now leaves a converged *prefix* rather than nothing. `recomputeExceptedAll()` is retained for the two integration tests that need single-step determinism on a tiny table, documented as not-for-production. Tests: `AsyncExceptionRecomputeChunkingTest` (5 cases pinning the traversal — sparse ids covered exactly once, half-open boundaries abutting without re-processing, no single range spanning the table) plus a `ExceptedFlagSqlAgreementIntegrationTest` case asserting the chunked statement assigns exactly what the atomic one does against a real database, with every flag pre-flipped so a skipped row cannot coincidentally match. Closes the `recomputeAll` lock-hold item open since the 2026-07-20 DB-pool work. OWASP: A01 reviewed — both new native queries bind parameters and take only primary-key boundaries from the preceding keyset read, on `@Async`/`@Scheduled` paths unreachable from any request.

- **Vulnerability SLA anchored to remediation availability (2026-08-24)** — `secman.vulnerability.use-patch-publication-date` now defaults to **true** (both `application.yml` and the `VulnerabilitySettings` data class, which had to be changed together — they disagreed, and a new `VulnerabilitySettingsDefaultTest` now pins both). Age is measured from when a **fix became available**, falling back to CrowdStrike detection age per row when no patch date is published. Rationale: detection age answers "how long have we known", which resets whenever a host is rebuilt or newly onboarded — a 2023 CVE on a month-old host read as a month old — while remediation age answers "how long could we have fixed this and did not" and does not reward re-imaging. This only became possible in the same change that made the field arrive at all: the CLI batch payload had been dropping `patchPublicationDate` entirely, so the flag was inert on the production import path, and the ad-hoc lookup path never populated the field either (its DTO construction set neither publication date, so "persist it on save" persisted null forever — both now use the shared `FalconTimestamps` extractors). Two consequences documented rather than discovered later: (1) **overdue counts jump** on the first import after the change, since a patch date is normally much earlier than the detection date, so expect an outsized notification run; (2) **it is a one-way door** — `first_seen_at` is preserved as `min(prior, new)` across re-imports (the property that stops a re-import resetting the SLA clock), so once an import writes the older patch date, setting the flag back to false does **not** restore the previous anchors. A genuine revert is `UPDATE vulnerability SET first_seen_at = NULL WHERE source = 'CROWDSTRIKE'` plus a full re-import with the flag off. `requirePatchPublicationDate` stays **false** and is pinned by test: despite the near-identical name it is a *filter*, not an anchor, and enabling it would drop every vulnerability with no published patch date — hiding risk rather than re-dating it. Nothing changes until the next import; existing rows keep their current anchors. `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md` §Timestamp fix, `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md`.

- **CrowdStrike date semantics: three dates untangled (2026-08-24)** — reported as "the import is wrong: a 2023 CVE cannot be only 226 days old". Investigation showed the arithmetic was right and the *meaning* was not, plus four real defects underneath. Falcon's `created_timestamp` is when Spotlight created that finding **on that host**, and it creates every finding against a package in one batch — so a host legitimately shows one identical age across dozens of CVEs. Confirmed on live data: `detectedAt` clusters (80 rows on one date, 60 on another) while the newly captured `cve.published_date` spreads across dozens. Also confirmed that a CVE's ID year is its *reservation* year — `CVE-2023-53178` in this estate has `published_date = 2025-09-15` — so "a 2023 CVE can't be 62 days old" was never a sound inference; the data to see that simply was not being captured. Fixes: (1) **`extractPatchPublicationDate` asked `cve.published_date` FIRST**, so the column named for a patch — and used as the SLA anchor when `VULN_USE_PATCH_PUBLICATION_DATE=true` — usually held the CVE *disclosure* date, silently answering "how long since a fix existed?" with "how long since the CVE was published". Genuine remediation dates (`remediation.vendor_release_date`, `remediation.published_date`) now win; the CVE fields are kept as the **last** resort rather than removed, because `require-patch-publication-date` filters imports on this being non-null and narrowing it would have silently dropped rows — nothing that was non-null before becomes null. (2) **Timezone bug**: `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityService.parseDetectionTimestamp` (the ad-hoc lookup behind the reported screen) parsed `"2026-01-10T22:18:26Z"` by *stripping* the `Z` and handing the rest to `LocalDateTime.parse`, relabelling a UTC instant as system-local instead of converting it — a whole-day shift across midnight, since age is `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between`. There were **four** copies of Falcon date parsing, one correct; all now delegate to one new `FalconTimestamps`, which also returns **null rather than `now()`** for an absent/unreadable date (defaulting to now reads as "detected today" = zero days = never overdue, a security miss dressed as a formatting fallback). (3) **The high-volume CLI batch payload dropped every date**: `/api/crowdstrike/servers/import` hand-built a map of `cveId`/`severity`/`affectedProduct`/`daysOpen` only, so `patchPublicationDate` was always null on the main import path and `VULN_USE_PATCH_PUBLICATION_DATE` could never take effect there at all. It now also sends `detectedAt` and both publication dates, and the backend prefers `detectedAt` over re-deriving `importTimestamp − daysOpen` — the same cross-clock, twice-truncated reconstruction shape as the 2026-08-21 reconcile incident (`daysOpen` is still sent, and the reconstruction retained, so an older CLI keeps working). (4) Saving from the ad-hoc lookup dropped `patch_publication_date` entirely. New `cve_published_date` column (V259, nullable, not backfilled — the import is delete-then-insert, so rows acquire it on the next run) surfaced on the lookup page as a **CVE Published** column, with "Days Open" renamed to **Detected (days)** and tooltipped as "not the age of the CVE". Tests: `CrowdStrikeTimestampParsingTest` (8 cases pinning the timezone contract and unknown-stays-null), `FalconDateExtractionTest` (6 cases pinning the preference order *and* the deliberate CVE fallback). Three unrelated pre-existing failures that had been red on `main` were also fixed to get a green build: `ResponseControllerAccessControlTest` (four `Cannot infer type for type parameter 'O'` — backend test sources did not compile at all), `InstalledProductListServiceTest` ×2 (mockk had no stub for a `countProductsByServer` call the service gained), and `VulnerabilityServicePreviewIntegrationTest` (reflection lookup missing the `includeInstallerFindings` parameter added by product classification). `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md` §Timestamp fix.

- **EOL mails carry the affected-systems table (2026-08-24)** — both EOL mail paths now embed the same table the product drilldown page shows, rendered by one new `EolFindingTableRenderer`: System, Type, Cloud account, **Cloud instance**, AD domain, Version, Release cycle, End of support, Status (plus Component for the owner notification, which spans many products; the broadcast is one product, so that column would be a constant). Previously the "Contact affected owners" broadcast (`/vulnerabilities/eol/products/{product}`) sent only the admin's free-text message with **no findings data at all**, and `secman send-eol-notifications` sent a 4-column Component/Version/Cycle/EOL table with no account, instance, domain, type or status — a recipient mapped to a whole AWS account could not tell which system or which account a row belonged to. Pieces: (1) **`cloudInstanceId` denormalized onto `eol_finding`** (V258, nullable, populated by `EolScanService` at both `ASSET_*` insertion sites exactly as `assetName`/`cloudAccountId`/`assetOwner` already are) and surfaced on `EolFindingResponse`, the page table and the CSV export so page, CSV and mail agree; deliberately **not backfilled** — the scan is delete-then-insert, so existing rows acquire it on the next `eol-sync` and read `-` until then; (2) **per-recipient scoping of the broadcast** — `EolBroadcastRecipientResolver.resolve` now returns `EolBroadcastRecipient(user, assetIds)` instead of `List<User>`, carrying the asset ids that made each user a recipient, and `EmailBroadcastService` renders only those rows into that recipient's copy. That linkage (owner, manual creator, scan uploader, AWS-account mapping, AD-domain mapping) is criteria 3/4/5/6/8 of §Unified Asset Access, hence provably a subset of what the recipient may already see (§A01) at **zero extra access queries** and with no way to drift from the rule that produced the recipient; sending one shared table would have disclosed other tenants' hostnames and account ids to every owner on the list. Manually-entered Cc addresses ride along on the owner's message and see that owner's rows only; (3) **bounded output** — rows and count are both taken at the query (`findByComponentNameForAssets` page of 200 + `countByComponentNameForAssets`), never fetched whole and sliced in Kotlin (§A04), and the remainder is disclosed in the table footer rather than silently truncated; (4) **one escaping sink** — the renderer escapes at assembly and strips CR/LF from the text part, replacing `EolNotificationService`'s private `escapeHtml`/`sanitizeForText` (which also escaped *before* truncating, so a 512-char cut could split an entity); the table is generated server-side at send time and never passes `EmailBroadcastService.sanitizeBroadcastHtml`, whose safelist strips every attribute except `a[href|title]` and would have removed the inline styles mail clients need. The compose modal now says the table is appended automatically and is scoped per recipient. Unrelated pre-existing breakage fixed to reach a green build: `ResponseControllerAccessControlTest` failed to compile on `main` (four `Cannot infer type for type parameter 'O'` on single-arg `exchange(...)`), so backend test sources did not build at all. `docs/EOL.md` §5.1.

- **CrowdStrike morning over-deletion fixes (2026-08-21 incident: 727,637 rows)** — every morning the post-import reconcile sweep deleted far too many vulnerability rows. Root cause from the prod log: the CLI's cutoff arrived timezone-skewed (>1h in the backend's future), the old guard fell back to `backendNow − 30min`, and because the import ran longer than 30 minutes the sweep judged everything the run imported in its first half-hour "stale" and deleted it — 727,637 rows in one statement, aborted=false. Fixes, layered: (1) **cutoff translation** — the CLI now sends `clientNow`; the backend measures the clock offset and translates `importStartedAt` into its own clock, and without `clientNow` a future cutoff **aborts** the sweep (delete nothing) instead of guessing; (2) **failure-aware sweep scope** — hosts whose Falcon Stage-2 batch failed/was truncated (`StreamingImportResult.failedHosts`) or whose backend POST/per-server transaction failed (`BatchStorageResult.failedHostnames`, `ImportStatisticsDto.failedHostnames`) are excluded from `queriedHosts`, since their un-refreshed rows were never fetched, not remediated; (3) **percentage brake** `CROWDSTRIKE_RECONCILE_MAX_DELETE_PERCENT` (default 20, 100 disables) over the resolved scope, fail-CLOSED on count errors — the zero-refresh brake only catches fully-empty runs; (4) **scoped per-host replace** — `importVulnerabilitiesForServer` no longer wipes every row on the asset: it deletes `source=CROWDSTRIKE` rows at the batch's `runSeverities` (new optional DTO field; source-only fallback for old callers), so MEDIUM/LOW and XLSX/nmap/manual rows survive, and a batch whose rows are ALL filtered out (blank CVE / missing patch date) skips the delete instead of committing delete-without-reinsert; (5) **stale-asset cleanup correctness** — rule A now vetoes assets with a recent `crowdStrikeAgentSeenAt` (a fully-patched host with a live sensor never refreshes `crowdStrikeLastImportedAt`), brake numerator and deletion use one shared cutoff and the same query, and the brake fails closed when the tracked-asset count is unavailable; (6) **observability** — reconcile audit columns on `crowdstrike_reconcile_job` (V257: queried/resolved/excluded counts, stale candidates, refreshed, dry_run), `--reconcile-dry-run` CLI flag, per-host replace logging at INFO, a `CROWDSTRIKE_RECONCILE_ABORTED` chat-notification event, and the MV refresh `triggered_by` insert no longer dies on over-length reasons (`.take(50)`, the log's second error). `scripts/import.sh` `--last-seen-days` regression 1→30 fixed (comment already said 30). `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md` §CrowdStrike reconcile sweep.
- **Apple `container` database selection (`--db`)** — `secman-container.sh up` now takes `--db container|host|none` (plus `--db-host/--db-port/--db-name`; `--with-db`/`--no-db` are aliases for the first and last). `container`, the default, runs the in-container MariaDB and publishes it on :3306; `host` runs none and points the stack at the MariaDB already installed on the Mac; `none` leaves `DB_CONNECT` to `pass-cli`. `host` was previously not reachable at all: the egress policy carries only 80/443/22 to allow-set addresses, so port 3306 to the Mac was refused with no rule capable of permitting it. The entrypoint now settles the mode **before** the firewall is built, resolves the Mac's address (it is the container's default gateway, which only the container can see), and writes the result to `/run/secman-dev/db/env` — the single file the firewall, `devctl` and every login shell read, so the iptables rule and the JDBC URL cannot disagree, including after a `refresh-egress` that inherits none of the entrypoint's environment. The rule is deliberately narrow: one address, one port, outside the allow-set (which is only ever matched on 80/443/22), and the address must be private — a public one is refused unless `SECMAN_DEV_DB_ALLOW_PUBLIC=1`, so a convenience flag cannot become general 3306 egress. The choice is made effective rather than advisory: `/etc/profile.d/secman-dev.sh` exports the resulting `DB_CONNECT` (plus the throwaway `DB_USERNAME`/`DB_PASSWORD` in `container` mode only), and `scripts/startbackenddev.sh` now honours a preset `DB_CONNECT` and falls back to `pass://Test/SECMAN/DB_CONNECT` when it is unset — unchanged behaviour on a Mac. `devctl db status` / `secman-container.sh db` report the mode, the URL and a live reachability probe, and name the three silent failure modes of `--db host` in order (server not running, bound to 127.0.0.1 only, no grant for the container's subnet); `devctl db start` refuses outside `container` mode rather than raising a second server behind a URL that names a different one. Every value that reaches an iptables rule or a JDBC URL goes through a closed character allowlist at both ends (§A03). `docs/APPLE_CONTAINER_DEV.md` §Choosing the database.

- **Apple `container` shielded dev environment (macOS/Apple silicon)** — `./scripts/container/secman-container.sh` builds and drives one long-lived Apple `container` VM that carries the whole toolchain (Temurin 25, Gradle 9.7.0, Node 24, Go 1.24, uv/Python 3.13, MariaDB 11.4, nginx) plus Claude Code, Kimi CLI and `pass-cli`, so the agents run inside a shield rather than on the developer's Mac. Three properties are the point. **One host path**: the source tree passed with `--src` is the only bind mount; the Gradle/npm caches, the agent state, the Proton Pass session and the MariaDB data directory live in named volumes — invisible to macOS, faster than virtiofs, and no widening of the exposure the container exists to narrow. `up` refuses `/`, `/Users`, `$HOME` and friends rather than trusting the caller to notice. **Egress by iptables alone, deliberately without a proxy**: `OUTPUT` policy `DROP`, and the only ways out are loopback, replies on established connections, DNS to the resolvers in `/etc/resolv.conf`, and TCP on 80/443/22 to an address in the allow-set. That set is built from the allowlist's hostnames resolved to their A records, its address/CIDR literals, and GitHub's published ranges from `api.github.com/meta` (a service across that many prefixes cannot be covered by resolving a few names); it is held in an `ipset` where the kernel has one — a single hash lookup per packet and an atomic swap on refresh — and in a plain rule chain where it does not, both probed rather than assumed because Apple's kernel is trimmed. The consequence is stated rather than buried: filtering is by **address, not name**, so anything else answering on an allowlisted address is reachable, and an address that rotates out of DNS stays permitted until the next refresh while its replacement is not. The second half is handled by re-resolving every 30 minutes (`SECMAN_EGRESS_REFRESH_MINUTES`), without which a container left running overnight starts failing npm and Maven downloads for reasons that look nothing like a firewall; the first half is inherent to packet-layer filtering. Denials `REJECT` rather than `DROP` so a blocked tool fails immediately instead of hanging, and a rate-limited `LOG` rule plus the reject counter are the record of what was refused now that there is no proxy log. Three guards fail closed: the container **refuses to start** if a non-allowlisted host is reachable, an allowlist that renders to nothing is refused, and a resolution round in which more than half the names fail is refused as broken DNS rather than installed as a policy that reaches almost nothing. The allowlist covers both agents, Proton, GitHub, Gradle/Maven/Google/JetBrains/Adoptium, npm, Go, PyPI, Playwright, Debian/MariaDB apt, and the hosts the app itself calls (`endoflife.date`, `api.crowdstrike.com` and its regional siblings, `openrouter.ai`, `hooks.slack.com`, `api.telegram.org`, `acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org`); `SECMAN_HOST` and AWS's regional endpoints are deliberately absent, since neither can be guessed. **Ports 8080/4321/443/3306** come back to the Mac, with nginx terminating TLS on 443 in front of both services because the `secman_auth` cookie is `Secure` and a plain-HTTP dev origin produces a login that silently never persists. Apple-specific behaviour is handled rather than documented-around: the default kernel has no working nftables, so `iptables-legacy` is pinned explicitly (a silent fall-through to the nft backend would fail *open*); IPv6 is incomplete, so it is disabled and all `ip6tables` policies set to `DROP`; there is no privileged mode, so exactly `NET_ADMIN` + `NET_RAW` are added; `--publish` needs macOS 26 and the script says so on 15; options must precede the image name; macOS reserves ports below 1024 for root, so `up` probes and falls back to publishing `:443` on `8443`; virtiofs presents the Mac's uid (501, not 1000), so the entrypoint creates `dev` with the uid/gid that actually own `/workspace`. Because there is no proxy, nothing in the container needs `HTTP_PROXY` or `-Dhttps.proxyHost` — no JVM banner on every start, and no tool that quietly ignores those variables and behaves differently from the rest. `pass-cli` uses `PROTON_PASS_KEY_PROVIDER=file` (there is no OS keyring in the VM) with the session on a named volume, so `pass-cli login --interactive` is a one-time step and no Proton state ever touches the Mac's filesystem or Keychain. The `dev` user has no sudo: the firewall and its allowlist are root-owned, so an agent session cannot dismantle the shield it runs in. Values that reach SQL identifiers or an OpenSSL subject go through a closed character allowlist first (§A03), and `--allow-domain` entries clear a strict hostname/CIDR regex before they can reach an `iptables -d` argument. Full reference: `docs/APPLE_CONTAINER_DEV.md`.

- **Public standard download: any standard, any release, over a plain GET** — the unauthenticated `/requirements/download` page could export the whole corpus or one use case, but not a *standard*, and there was no way to ask for "the latest released version of the IT/OT Security standard" from a script. `GET /api/requirements/export/{docx,xlsx}` now take four optional query parameters — `standard` (exact name, case-insensitive), `standardId` (wins if both given), `release` (`latest`, or an exact version) and the pre-existing `releaseId` — all `IS_ANONYMOUS`, matching the four public export endpoints that already existed. A standard has **no direct link to requirements**: `Standard.useCases` joins `Requirement.usecases`, so a standard selects every requirement tagged with any of its use cases, de-duplicated and ordered by chapter — the same rule `StandardController.getStandardRequirements` applies. Release-scoped standard exports filter `RequirementSnapshot.usecaseIdsSnapshot` through `ReleaseRequirementScopeService`, so a historical download is reproducible rather than re-derived from live rows. Three failure modes fail loudly rather than degrading: `release=latest` with **no ACTIVE release** is a 404 and never silently serves the live corpus ("the latest release" and "whatever is in the editor" are different answers); `releaseId` and `release` identifying different releases is a 400 rather than one silently winning; and a standard with **no use cases mapped** returns `{"message": "No requirements found for this standard"}` rather than falling through to everything, so a half-configured standard cannot publish the full corpus by accident. Name matching is a bound-parameter `LOWER(s.name) = LOWER(:name)` fetch-join (`Standard.useCases` is LAZY, so a detached read would throw); an over-long name is rejected before the query runs. The standard name reaches `Content-Disposition`, so `StandardExportScopeService.exportFilename` strips it to `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, collapses repeated dots and drops a leading one — `IT/OT Security` becomes `ITOT_Security`, `../../etc/passwd` becomes `etcpasswd` — and the xlsx endpoint gained the `"`/CR/LF strip the docx path already had. A new slim `GET /api/standards/public` returns `{id, name}` only so the picker works logged out; `GET /api/standards` stays `IS_AUTHENTICATED`, keeping descriptions, use-case mappings and timestamps behind auth. The download page gains a third *Complete Standard* card that reuses the existing release selector (which already lists every release plus "Current Version (Live)") and shows the equivalent name-based URL for the current selection, so the page documents its own API. `RequirementExportScope.STANDARD` was added for the template usage audit. **Not rate limited** — public document generation was already an unauthenticated CPU cost before this change and stays a reverse-proxy concern. Tests: `StandardExportScopeServiceTest` (25 unit), `PublicStandardExportIntegrationTest` (15, every request credential-free, including that `GET /api/standards` still 401s), `requirementDownloadUrl.test.ts` (8). See `docs/PUBLIC_STANDARD_DOWNLOAD.md`.
- **EOL matching for applications and frameworks: Java's nine distributions, the .NET family, and four rules that stop the estate being told supported software is dead** — the EOL dashboard showed operating systems only while `/products` plainly listed `.Net Framework 4.8` and `.NET Core 1.0`–`6.0`. The cause was not a missing data source: `EolSubjectType.ASSET_PRODUCT` and `scanInstalledProducts` already existed and were correct. `installed_product` was simply **empty at scan time** — it is fed by CrowdStrike **Discover** via the separate `secman installed-products` CLI, not by the Spotlight vulnerability import that fills `vulnerability.vulnerable_product_versions` behind `/products`. The first-ever Discover import landed 182,131 rows across 2,010 assets and the scan went from 304 findings to real coverage; **no new scan source was needed and none was added.** What *was* broken is matching, in four ways, each proven against the live inventory rather than inferred. **Java could not match at all**: endoflife.date publishes no generic `java` product — it publishes `oracle-jdk`, `amazon-corretto`, `eclipse-temurin`, `azul-zulu`, `microsoft-build-of-openjdk`, `redhat-build-of-openjdk`, `openjdk-builds-from-oracle`, `graalvm-ce` and `oracle-graalvm`, because Oracle JDK 8, Corretto 8 and Temurin 8 end on different dates — so the five curated aliases targeting `"java"` resolved to a key no product owned and were **dropped silently at index build time**, which is the documented behaviour for speculative targets and is exactly why the failure was invisible. Each spelling now maps to the distribution that ships it, an unidentifiable build produces no finding rather than borrowing another vendor's date, and where the name is ambiguous (`OpenJDK Platform 11`) the vendor decides — enabled by adding corporate suffixes (`Inc`, `Corporation`, `Ltd`, `GmbH`, `LLC`) to the noise tokens so `Oracle Corporation OpenJDK Platform` tokenizes to a usable alias prefix. **Legacy Java versions were unmatchable**: Java numbered releases `1.x` up to Java 8 and plainly `x` after, so `1.8.0.392` segments to `[1,8,0,392]` and prefix-matches no cycle; it is now rewritten to `8.0.392`, only for the Java distributions and only when the leading segment is exactly `1` (`1.4` → `4`, which no cycle carries, so it fails closed). **Labelled cycles matched by list order**: every `windows` cycle upstream carries an edition label (`10-1507`, `11-24h2-e-lts`) and cycle comparison keeps only the leading numeric run, so `10-1507` collapsed to `[10]` and the Windows Server 2022 build `10.0.20348.3451` prefix-matched it — **3,672 findings, 42 % of the total, reporting supported servers as end of life since 2017**, decided by nothing but release ordering. Labelled cycles are now skipped (`isNumericCycle`), because which edition a bare build number belongs to cannot be recovered without a build-to-release table the catalogue does not publish; Windows Server is unaffected, its cycles are plain numbers. **Distribution packages were judged against upstream lifecycles**: a packaging revision (`1.18.0-6ubuntu14.4`, `2026c-1.el8_10`, `3.4.1-11.amzn2`, `~esm1`) *proves* the support contract belongs to the distribution — Canonical still supports nginx 1.18 long after upstream dropped it — and a maintainer vendor (`Ubuntu Developers <ubuntu-devel-discuss@…>`) proves it even when the version looks plain, which is how the Ubuntu npm library `node-arrify 2.0.1-2` was reported as "Node.js 2, end of life". Both are rejected; Red Hat and Amazon Linux are deliberately **not** vendor-blocked because their packages carry `.el8`/`.amzn2` in the version and blocking the vendor would make `redhat-build-of-openjdk` unmatchable. Also curated: `Microsoft Windows Desktop Runtime - 8.0.21` is the .NET desktop runtime, and without an explicit entry the shorter `microsoft windows` alias captured it and reported **.NET 8 as Windows 8, EOL 2016**; and `ASP .Net Core` → `dotnet` (no product of its own upstream, its versions track .NET exactly), noting the alias is `asp net core` because tokenization strips the leading dot. Net effect on the live estate: 304 → **4,492 findings** (3,386 EOL, 1,106 approaching) with the Windows, Node-library and distro-package false-positive classes eliminated — Internet Explorer 11 (762), .NET 8 approaching (443), SQL Server 2016 (279), .NET 6 (165), Visual Studio 15.0/16.0/10.0, Splunk 8.1/9.0/9.2, and Oracle JDK 6/7/8/11 plus Corretto and Oracle's OpenJDK builds now reporting for the first time. Nine new matcher tests (EVM-015..023) pin every rule in both directions, including the exact Windows Server 2022 build number and the requirement that the OS path stay byte-identical; the 14 pre-existing cases still pass. **OWASP: A04 touched (matching correctness) — clean, 0 static findings**; the change is a pure function with no SQL, auth, I/O or HTML surface. Unrelated fix required to verify anything at all: `RequirementExportTemplateValidationServiceTest` referenced `org.apache.poi.xwpf.usermodel.HeaderFooterType`, which does not exist (it is `org.apache.poi.wp.usermodel`), and that single unresolved reference had been failing `compileTestKotlin` and therefore blocking the **entire** backend test suite since the requirement-export-template commit. With it fixed, `RequirementExportTemplateIntegrationTest.an uploaded template can be deactivated and activated again` failed — but on investigation the **endpoint is correct and the test was wrong**: `@MicronautTest` wraps each test in a transaction, so the injected repository holds one persistence context for the whole method while the controller commits in its own. The first `findById` is the initial load and reads the database; the second returns the **cached instance** and never sees the controller's write. Proven by instrumenting the assertion — the activate response body reported `ACTIVE` while the repository re-read reported `INACTIVE`. Fixed with the `entityManager.clear()` pattern already used by `StatisticsAggregateIntegrationTest` and `ExceptedFlagSqlAgreementIntegrationTest`, wrapped in a `rereadFromDb` helper whose KDoc records the trap: only the *second* read of an entity lies, so this failure mode reads exactly like a broken endpoint. Backend suite is green.
- **Company Word template for requirement exports: real release metadata, an in-place insertion point, a seeded example** — the template machinery already existed (`RequirementExportTemplate`, `/api/requirement-export-templates`, `templateMode=LATEST` already the export default) but nothing ever produced a templated document: no example shipped and nothing seeded one, so `LATEST` found no ACTIVE row and silently degraded to the built-in layout. Three things were wrong underneath. **Release metadata was faked** — `releaseVersion` was sliced out of the document title with `title.substringAfter("Release ")` and `releaseStatus` was hard-coded to `""`, so a cover page could never carry either; the `Release` entity is now threaded through `resolveRequirementExportData` → `exportWordDocument` → `createTemplatedWordDocument` and binds `${releaseName}`, `${releaseVersion}`, `${releaseDate}` (falling back to `createdAt`), `${releaseStatus}` and `${releaseDescription}` for real, with `${useCaseName}` from the `UseCase` entity. All resolve to `""` for a live (non-release) export — the same contract, told honestly. **`${requirements}` was not an insertion point** — it was replaced with an empty string and content always appended after a page break, so a template could not put a cover page before and an appendix after; it is now an anchor, with `appendRequirementContent` taking a paragraph factory and the templated path inserting via `XmlCursor` in front of the marker (a fresh cursor per insert, because POI invalidates it) before removing the marker paragraph. That removal indexes into `document.bodyElements`, **not** `getPosOfParagraph` — the latter counts paragraphs only, so on a template containing a table (a cover page usually does) the two disagree and the wrong element is deleted. Absent marker still falls back to appending, which is what `MissingPlaceholderBehavior.APPEND` means. **A marker in a table cell, header or footer cannot host body-level content**, so validation now rejects it in strict mode and warns in append mode rather than producing a silently wrong document. - **AWS account onboarding: welcome mail, direct and guided risk assessments** — the "new AWS account discovered → mail the owner and start an assessment" path becomes a three-mode capability, and the scoping decision moves to the person who actually knows. `WELCOME_ONLY` sends a welcome mail from a classpath template; `DIRECT` additionally starts an assessment for a use case the operator names (today's behaviour); `GUIDED` mails the owner a **one-time, expiring link** whose answers resolve through admin-configured rules into a *set* of use cases, and creates the assessment only on submit, scoped to the **union** of every matching rule. All three run from CLI (`--onboarding-mode`, `--welcome-email`, `--questionnaire-expiry-days` on `import` and `import-s3`), REST and MCP, all dry-runnable, plus a first-class `simulate-onboarding` verb (CLI + REST + MCP `simulate_account_onboarding`) that runs the whole path against a made-up account id and address — the *same* code path a real import runs, not a mock, which is what makes it a rehearsal and why it is rate limited, audited, and stamps every simulated mail with "this is a test, sent by <actor>". **The backward-compatibility contract is the load-bearing part**: a caller sending only `startRiskAssessment=true` — every `extensions/` client, `import-s3`, both existing E2E drivers — resolves to `DIRECT` **with no welcome mail**, byte-identical to before, reconciled in one function (`AccountOnboardingMode.resolve`); an explicit non-`DIRECT` mode combined with that flag is rejected, never guessed. **The matcher never decides**: it sees only choice ids (a BOOLEAN question is two choices, no second code path), every matching active rule contributes and nothing wins, `priorityOrder` is display order only, the single `isDefault` rule is consulted **after** everything else fails, and a resolution producing no requirements in the ACTIVE release is an error rather than an empty questionnaire. Answers that match nothing are **persisted** and the invite stays usable, so an admin can add the missing rule and the owner's original link still works. Rules are normalized tables, not a `ruleJson` blob (`DemandClassificationRule`'s precedent exists for a recursive condition; this one is a flat AND over choice ids, and the rule→use-case link needs real FK integrity). **The public questionnaire is the first genuinely unauthenticated write path in the codebase** and is treated as such: 256-bit `SecureRandom` token (not `UUID.randomUUID()`, because this token *creates* an assessment), single use enforced by a guarded UPDATE **claimed before** creation, 14-day expiry, a byte-identical 404 for malformed/unknown/expired/used/cancelled so the endpoint is no enumeration oracle, the account id **masked** to four digits and the owner email never returned, a new bounded fixed-window rate limiter with a dedicated failed-lookup bucket, `@Secured(IS_ANONYMOUS)` explicit on every method plus an `intercept-url-map` entry so a stale `secman_auth` cookie cannot 401 an owner out of their own link, and the full token never logged, never returned by any API, never printed by the CLI, never in an MCP result and never minted by a dry run — all asserted. Adding a reportable event is a `NotificationEventType` constant plus one publish call — the settings APIs, both settings UIs and the dispatcher all derive from the enum, so nothing else changes. Adding a transport is one client plus one branch, with no publisher touched. **Subscriptions are rows, not columns**: `user_notification_subscription (user_id, channel, event_type)` — so a new event type or a whole new channel costs no migration, "who wants X over Slack" is a single indexed lookup on the dispatch path, and one user can route CrowdStrike to Slack and AWS imports to Telegram. Telegram: the user's chat ID is always required (Telegram addresses a conversation, not a person), with the token being the user's personal bot if set, otherwise the workspace bot — so a personal bot keeps working even when workspace delivery is switched off. Every route acts on the caller's own settings — the user id comes from the token and is never read from the body. That round trip — not the magic-byte sniff — is the control that actually matters: it destroys polyglot payloads (a valid PNG with `<script>` appended still decodes as a PNG and would pass any header check) and strips EXIF/GPS metadata, verified by a dedicated test. The **dimension probe runs before `reader.read(0)`**, so a 2 MB PNG cannot decode into a multi-gigabyte `BufferedImage` and trip `-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` on the 1 GB heap; without that guard the endpoint would be a single-request kill switch. WEBP is deliberately **absent** from the allowlist (the JDK has no WEBP reader, so accepting it would mean storing bytes that were never decoded) — this costs nothing in practice because the frontend cropper exports its canvas as PNG, so WEBP/HEIC sources still work end to end. SVG is rejected three independent ways: not in the allowlist, `.svg` already in `SecurityService.DANGEROUS_EXTENSIONS`, and no SVG `ImageReader` exists. Only the JDK is used (`javax.imageio`/`java.awt.image`); `-Djava.awt.headless=true` was pinned in `applicationDefaultJvmArgs`. It took exclusive row locks on every `vulnerability` row (~1.8M in production) and, through its correlated subquery, read locks on `vulnerability_exception` — holding both for the entire 53–180s transaction. Every concurrent writer to either table then blocked until lock-wait-timeout: bulk exception delete/import, CrowdStrike imports, per-asset recomputes. `DeadlockRetry` absorbed the failure, which is exactly why it stayed hidden — but the *other* operation still paid the full timeout first, observed as ~40s per `delete_all_vulnerability_exceptions` in both E2E runs, contending with "Async full excepted recompute complete: 1824736 rows in 53481 ms". Fix: `AsyncExceptionRecompute.recomputeAllChunked` drives the recompute as bounded **keyset** chunks (`CHUNK_SIZE` 10,000) through the new `recomputeExceptedForIdRange(afterId, throughId)`, each in its own REQUIRES_NEW transaction with per-chunk `DeadlockRetry`. Lock hold per transaction drops from minutes to milliseconds, so competing writers interleave between chunks instead of queueing behind one lock set; a chunk that loses a race replays only its own id range instead of the whole statement. **Keyset, not fixed-width id stepping** — the CrowdStrike import is delete-then-insert per asset, so ids are sparse and `MAX(id)` runs far ahead of the row count, which would make blind stepping spend most iterations on empty ranges. The daily 03:00 `recomputeAllExceptedScheduled` now delegates to the same driver (its orphaned `selfProvider` removed), so the nightly pass stops reintroducing the hold. Chunking gives up atomicity, and that is argued rather than assumed: the operation is already `@Async`, its documented contract is already eventual ("rows stay visible until it lands", failures "non-fatal; standing sweeps will retry"), a mid-statement failure already left partial state, and readers evaluate `v.excepted = 0` per row without a cross-table snapshot — so no guarantee is lost, and a failure now leaves a converged *prefix* rather than nothing. `recomputeExceptedAll()` is retained for the two integration tests that need single-step determinism on a tiny table, documented as not-for-production. Tests: `AsyncExceptionRecomputeChunkingTest` (5 cases pinning the traversal — sparse ids covered exactly once, half-open boundaries abutting without re-processing, no single range spanning the table) plus a `ExceptedFlagSqlAgreementIntegrationTest` case asserting the chunked statement assigns exactly what the atomic one does against a real database, with every flag pre-flipped so a skipped row cannot coincidentally match. Closes the `recomputeAll` lock-hold item open since the 2026-07-20 DB-pool work. OWASP: A01 reviewed — both new native queries bind parameters and take only primary-key boundaries from the preceding keyset read, on `@Async`/`@Scheduled` paths unreachable from any request.

- **Vulnerability SLA anchored to remediation availability (2026-08-24)** — `secman.vulnerability.use-patch-publication-date` now defaults to **true** (both `application.yml` and the `VulnerabilitySettings` data class, which had to be changed together — they disagreed, and a new `VulnerabilitySettingsDefaultTest` now pins both). Age is measured from when a **fix became available**, falling back to CrowdStrike detection age per row when no patch date is published. Rationale: detection age answers "how long have we known", which resets whenever a host is rebuilt or newly onboarded — a 2023 CVE on a month-old host read as a month old — while remediation age answers "how long could we have fixed this and did not" and does not reward re-imaging. This only became possible in the same change that made the field arrive at all: the CLI batch payload had been dropping `patchPublicationDate` entirely, so the flag was inert on the production import path, and the ad-hoc lookup path never populated the field either (its DTO construction set neither publication date, so "persist it on save" persisted null forever — both now use the shared `FalconTimestamps` extractors). Two consequences documented rather than discovered later: (1) **overdue counts jump** on the first import after the change, since a patch date is normally much earlier than the detection date, so expect an outsized notification run; (2) **it is a one-way door** — `first_seen_at` is preserved as `min(prior, new)` across re-imports (the property that stops a re-import resetting the SLA clock), so once an import writes the older patch date, setting the flag back to false does **not** restore the previous anchors. A genuine revert is `UPDATE vulnerability SET first_seen_at = NULL WHERE source = 'CROWDSTRIKE'` plus a full re-import with the flag off. `requirePatchPublicationDate` stays **false** and is pinned by test: despite the near-identical name it is a *filter*, not an anchor, and enabling it would drop every vulnerability with no published patch date — hiding risk rather than re-dating it. Nothing changes until the next import; existing rows keep their current anchors. `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md` §Timestamp fix, `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md`.

- **CrowdStrike date semantics: three dates untangled (2026-08-24)** — reported as "the import is wrong: a 2023 CVE cannot be only 226 days old". Investigation showed the arithmetic was right and the *meaning* was not, plus four real defects underneath. Falcon's `created_timestamp` is when Spotlight created that finding **on that host**, and it creates every finding against a package in one batch — so a host legitimately shows one identical age across dozens of CVEs. Confirmed on live data: `detectedAt` clusters (80 rows on one date, 60 on another) while the newly captured `cve.published_date` spreads across dozens. Also confirmed that a CVE's ID year is its *reservation* year — `CVE-2023-53178` in this estate has `published_date = 2025-09-15` — so "a 2023 CVE can't be 62 days old" was never a sound inference; the data to see that simply was not being captured. Fixes: (1) **`extractPatchPublicationDate` asked `cve.published_date` FIRST**, so the column named for a patch — and used as the SLA anchor when `VULN_USE_PATCH_PUBLICATION_DATE=true` — usually held the CVE *disclosure* date, silently answering "how long since a fix existed?" with "how long since the CVE was published". Genuine remediation dates (`remediation.vendor_release_date`, `remediation.published_date`) now win; the CVE fields are kept as the **last** resort rather than removed, because `require-patch-publication-date` filters imports on this being non-null and narrowing it would have silently dropped rows — nothing that was non-null before becomes null. (2) **Timezone bug**: `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityService.parseDetectionTimestamp` (the ad-hoc lookup behind the reported screen) parsed `"2026-01-10T22:18:26Z"` by *stripping* the `Z` and handing the rest to `LocalDateTime.parse`, relabelling a UTC instant as system-local instead of converting it — a whole-day shift across midnight, since age is `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between`. There were **four** copies of Falcon date parsing, one correct; all now delegate to one new `FalconTimestamps`, which also returns **null rather than `now()`** for an absent/unreadable date (defaulting to now reads as "detected today" = zero days = never overdue, a security miss dressed as a formatting fallback). (3) **The high-volume CLI batch payload dropped every date**: `/api/crowdstrike/servers/import` hand-built a map of `cveId`/`severity`/`affectedProduct`/`daysOpen` only, so `patchPublicationDate` was always null on the main import path and `VULN_USE_PATCH_PUBLICATION_DATE` could never take effect there at all. It now also sends `detectedAt` and both publication dates, and the backend prefers `detectedAt` over re-deriving `importTimestamp − daysOpen` — the same cross-clock, twice-truncated reconstruction shape as the 2026-08-21 reconcile incident (`daysOpen` is still sent, and the reconstruction retained, so an older CLI keeps working). (4) Saving from the ad-hoc lookup dropped `patch_publication_date` entirely. New `cve_published_date` column (V259, nullable, not backfilled — the import is delete-then-insert, so rows acquire it on the next run) surfaced on the lookup page as a **CVE Published** column, with "Days Open" renamed to **Detected (days)** and tooltipped as "not the age of the CVE". Tests: `CrowdStrikeTimestampParsingTest` (8 cases pinning the timezone contract and unknown-stays-null), `FalconDateExtractionTest` (6 cases pinning the preference order *and* the deliberate CVE fallback). Three unrelated pre-existing failures that had been red on `main` were also fixed to get a green build: `ResponseControllerAccessControlTest` (four `Cannot infer type for type parameter 'O'` — backend test sources did not compile at all), `InstalledProductListServiceTest` ×2 (mockk had no stub for a `countProductsByServer` call the service gained), and `VulnerabilityServicePreviewIntegrationTest` (reflection lookup missing the `includeInstallerFindings` parameter added by product classification). `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md` §Timestamp fix.

- **EOL mails carry the affected-systems table (2026-08-24)** — both EOL mail paths now embed the same table the product drilldown page shows, rendered by one new `EolFindingTableRenderer`: System, Type, Cloud account, **Cloud instance**, AD domain, Version, Release cycle, End of support, Status (plus Component for the owner notification, which spans many products; the broadcast is one product, so that column would be a constant). Previously the "Contact affected owners" broadcast (`/vulnerabilities/eol/products/{product}`) sent only the admin's free-text message with **no findings data at all**, and `secman send-eol-notifications` sent a 4-column Component/Version/Cycle/EOL table with no account, instance, domain, type or status — a recipient mapped to a whole AWS account could not tell which system or which account a row belonged to. Pieces: (1) **`cloudInstanceId` denormalized onto `eol_finding`** (V258, nullable, populated by `EolScanService` at both `ASSET_*` insertion sites exactly as `assetName`/`cloudAccountId`/`assetOwner` already are) and surfaced on `EolFindingResponse`, the page table and the CSV export so page, CSV and mail agree; deliberately **not backfilled** — the scan is delete-then-insert, so existing rows acquire it on the next `eol-sync` and read `-` until then; (2) **per-recipient scoping of the broadcast** — `EolBroadcastRecipientResolver.resolve` now returns `EolBroadcastRecipient(user, assetIds)` instead of `List<User>`, carrying the asset ids that made each user a recipient, and `EmailBroadcastService` renders only those rows into that recipient's copy. That linkage (owner, manual creator, scan uploader, AWS-account mapping, AD-domain mapping) is criteria 3/4/5/6/8 of §Unified Asset Access, hence provably a subset of what the recipient may already see (§A01) at **zero extra access queries** and with no way to drift from the rule that produced the recipient; sending one shared table would have disclosed other tenants' hostnames and account ids to every owner on the list. Manually-entered Cc addresses ride along on the owner's message and see that owner's rows only; (3) **bounded output** — rows and count are both taken at the query (`findByComponentNameForAssets` page of 200 + `countByComponentNameForAssets`), never fetched whole and sliced in Kotlin (§A04), and the remainder is disclosed in the table footer rather than silently truncated; (4) **one escaping sink** — the renderer escapes at assembly and strips CR/LF from the text part, replacing `EolNotificationService`'s private `escapeHtml`/`sanitizeForText` (which also escaped *before* truncating, so a 512-char cut could split an entity); the table is generated server-side at send time and never passes `EmailBroadcastService.sanitizeBroadcastHtml`, whose safelist strips every attribute except `a[href|title]` and would have removed the inline styles mail clients need.
